chapters.n: Numbers opens a month after the tabernacle was set up, still at Sinai. Its Hebrew name, Bemidbar, means “In the Wilderness”—the setting for Israel’s forty years of wandering.

f.w: the first day of the second month

f.g: The desert region around Mount Sinai.

chapters.n: God commands a census of the whole community by clans and families. The English title “Numbers” comes from the two censuses in this book (chapters 1 and 26).
The count includes men twenty and older who could serve in the army. Israel is being organized to march toward and enter the promised land.
A leader from each tribe will assist Moses and Aaron. Shared leadership is a recurring pattern in God’s work.

f.w: head of the house of his fathers
f.g: Leader of an ancestral family group.

chapters.n: The tribal leaders are listed, starting with Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn. Elizur’s name means “my God is a rock.”
For Simeon, Shelumiel, whose name means “God is my peace.”
For Judah, Nahshon son of Amminadab. Nahshon was Aaron’s brother-in-law and an ancestor of King David and of Jesus.
For Issachar, Nethaneel, meaning “God has given.”
For Zebulun, Eliab son of Helon.
Joseph’s descendants form two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, because Jacob adopted Joseph’s sons as his own. This is why there are still twelve tribes without Levi.

f.g: Elishama was the grandfather of Joshua.

chapters.n: For Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni.
For Dan, Ahiezer, meaning “my brother is help.”
For Asher, Pagiel son of Ocran.
For Gad, Eliasaph son of Deuel (called Reuel in Numbers 2:14, a common spelling variation).
For Naphtali, Ahira son of Enan—completing the list of twelve.
These were respected tribal leaders, “heads of thousands”—large clan divisions.

f.g: Called or chosen ones; leaders summoned from the congregation.

chapters.n: Moses and Aaron gather the named leaders.
The people register by ancestry. Knowing one’s lineage determined land inheritance and covenant identity.
Moses carries out the census just as God commanded.
Reuben, Jacob’s eldest son, is counted first. The formula repeats for each tribe, showing that every family was carefully accounted for.
Reuben numbers 46,500 men of fighting age.
Simeon, Jacob’s second son, is counted next.
Simeon has 59,300—but by the second census (Numbers 26:14) it will shrink dramatically to 22,200.

f.w: fifty and nine thousand and three hundred

chapters.n: Gad, son of Jacob through Zilpah, Leah’s servant, is counted.
Gad numbers 45,650.
Judah, the tribe of kings, is counted.
Judah is the largest tribe: 74,600. “Threescore” means sixty, so “threescore and fourteen” is seventy-four.
Issachar, Leah’s fifth son, is counted.
Issachar numbers 54,400.
Zebulun, Leah’s sixth son, is counted.
Zebulun numbers 57,400.
Ephraim, Joseph’s younger son, is counted. Jacob had blessed him above his older brother.
Ephraim numbers 40,500. Latter-day Saints see Ephraim as having a special birthright role in the latter-day gathering.
Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, is counted. Lehi was a descendant of Manasseh.
Manasseh numbers 32,200, the smallest tribe at this point.
Benjamin, Rachel’s younger son, is counted.
Benjamin numbers 35,400.
Dan, son of Rachel’s servant Bilhah, is counted.
Dan numbers 62,700, the second largest tribe.
Asher, son of Zilpah, is counted.
Asher numbers 41,500.
Naphtali, son of Bilhah, is counted last.
Naphtali numbers 53,400.
The census was done by Moses, Aaron, and the twelve tribal leaders together.
The grand total of fighting men is about to be given.

603,550 men of fighting age. With women, children, and elders, the total population would be much larger. Some scholars debate how to read these large numbers, but the text presents a mighty people fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty

chapters.n: The Levites are not included in this military census.
Moses had received a separate instruction about them.
Levi is not to be counted with the other tribes. Their calling was different.
The Levites are appointed over the tabernacle and its furnishings. They carry it, serve in it, and camp around it. Their service anticipates priesthood duties of caring for sacred things.

f.g: The tabernacle, which housed the “testimony”—the covenant tablets.

chapters.n: Only Levites may take down and set up the tabernacle; any unauthorized person who approaches will die. Holy things required authorized hands.
The other tribes camp in assigned places, each under its own banner.

f.g: A banner or flag identifying a group.

chapters.n: The Levites camp around the tabernacle as a protective buffer, preventing anyone from approaching carelessly and bringing God’s wrath.
Israel obeys fully—a hopeful start to the book.
After counting the people, the Lord tells Moses and Aaron how to arrange the camp. Order in the camp reflected the order of heaven.
Each tribe camps under its own banner, facing the tabernacle at a respectful distance. God’s dwelling stood at the very center of Israel’s life.

f.g: A large banner for a group of three tribes.
A smaller flag or sign for a family group.

chapters.n: Judah camps on the east, toward the sunrise—the place of honor, facing the tabernacle entrance. Nahshon leads them.

f.w: east side toward the rising of the sun

chapters.n: Judah’s army numbers 74,600, as in the census.
Issachar camps next to Judah, led by Nethaneel.
Issachar numbers 54,400.
Zebulun completes Judah’s group, under Eliab. All three tribes on the east descend from Leah.
Zebulun numbers 57,400.
Judah’s camp totals 186,400 and leads the march. “Fourscore” means eighty.
Reuben’s camp is on the south, led by Elizur.
Reuben numbers 46,500.
Simeon camps beside Reuben, under Shelumiel.
Simeon numbers 59,300.
Gad completes the southern group, led by Eliasaph son of Reuel (Deuel in chapter 1—the Hebrew letters d and r look very similar).
Gad numbers 45,650.
Reuben’s camp totals 151,450 and marches second.
The tabernacle and the Levites travel in the middle, protected on every side. God’s presence moved with His people at the heart of the column.

f.w: in the midst of the camp

chapters.n: Ephraim’s camp is on the west, led by Elishama. This group is all Rachel’s descendants.
Ephraim numbers 40,500.
Manasseh camps beside Ephraim, led by Gamaliel.

f.g: The name means “reward of God”; a later Pharisee bore the same name.

chapters.n: Manasseh numbers 32,200.
Benjamin, Rachel’s other son, completes the western group under Abidan.
Benjamin numbers 35,400.
Ephraim’s camp totals 108,100 and marches third.
Dan’s camp is on the north, led by Ahiezer.
Dan numbers 62,700.
Asher camps beside Dan, led by Pagiel.
Asher numbers 41,500.
Naphtali completes the northern group under Ahira. These three tribes descend from the handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah.
Naphtali numbers 53,400.
Dan’s camp totals 157,600 and serves as the rear guard.
The four camps add up to the same 603,550 counted in chapter 1. Picture a great square with the tabernacle at the center.

f.w: six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty

chapters.n: The Levites are counted separately, in chapter 3.
Israel obeys, camping and traveling in perfect order by tribe and family.
The narrator introduces the family records of Aaron and Moses, the priestly line, at the time God spoke at Sinai.

f.g: Family records or line of descent.

chapters.n: Aaron had four sons: Nadab (the firstborn), Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
All four were anointed and consecrated as priests to serve with their father.
Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire and left no children. So Eleazar and Ithamar served under Aaron’s supervision. Priesthood authority must be exercised as God directs.

f.g: During Aaron’s lifetime, under his oversight.

chapters.n: The Lord now speaks to Moses about the Levites.
The tribe of Levi is presented to Aaron to assist him. Moses and Aaron were themselves Levites.

f.w: Bring the tribe of Levi near

chapters.n: They serve both Aaron and the whole community by caring for the tabernacle. The Levites did practical work so the priests could perform the sacred ordinances.

f.g: Carry out his duties and guard what he oversees.

chapters.n: They look after the tabernacle’s furnishings on behalf of all Israel. Latter-day Saints recognize in Levi’s service the Aaronic Priesthood, which still assists in sacred ordinances today.
The Levites are given wholly to Aaron and his sons out of all Israel.
Only Aaron and his sons hold the priest’s office. Any unauthorized person who approaches the sacred duties faces death.

f.g: Here, anyone not authorized, even another Israelite.

chapters.n: The Lord gives the reason the Levites are set apart.
God takes the Levites in place of every firstborn son in Israel. The whole tribe stands as a substitute, belonging especially to Him.

f.g: Opens the womb—that is, the firstborn.

chapters.n: The firstborn belonged to God since the Passover night, when He spared Israel’s firstborn while Egypt’s died. Their lives were, in a sense, purchased by the Passover lamb.
God commands another census in the wilderness of Sinai.
All Levite males from one month old are counted—not just men of fighting age, because this count is for sacred service and redemption, not war.

f.w: from a month old and upward

chapters.n: Moses counts them as commanded.
Levi had three sons, whose descendants form the three Levite clans: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Gershon’s sons were Libni and Shimei.
Kohath’s sons were Amram (father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam), Izehar, Hebron, and Uzziel.

f.g: Korah, who later rebelled, descended from Izehar.

chapters.n: Merari’s sons were Mahli and Mushi. These form the Levite family structure.
The Gershonite clans are the Libnites and Shimites.
Gershonite males number 7,500.
They camp on the west side, behind the tabernacle.
Their leader is Eliasaph son of Lael (a different man from the Gadite leader of the same name).
The Gershonites care for the fabrics: the tabernacle curtains, the tent, its coverings, and the entrance screen.
They also care for the courtyard curtains, the courtyard entrance curtain, and the cords.

f.g: The open courtyard surrounding the tabernacle.

chapters.n: The Kohathite clans are named. Moses’s and Aaron’s own family, the Amramites, belong to Kohath.
Kohathite males number 8,600. They are trusted with the most sacred objects.

f.w: keeping the charge of the sanctuary

chapters.n: They camp on the south side of the tabernacle.
Their leader is Elizaphan son of Uzziel, Moses’s cousin.
The Kohathites carry the holiest furnishings: the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, and the vessels. Only after priests covered them could the Kohathites carry them.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son, supervises all the Levite leaders and the care of the sanctuary.
The Merarite clans are the Mahlites and Mushites.
Merarite males number 6,200. (The three clan totals add to 22,300, slightly more than the 22,000 in verse 39; many explanations have been proposed, including a copying variation.)
Their leader is Zuriel son of Abihail; they camp on the north side.
The Merarites carry the heavy structural parts: frames, crossbars, posts, and bases.

f.g: Bases into which the posts fit.

chapters.n: They also carry the courtyard posts, bases, tent pegs, and ropes. Every role, even the humblest, was essential.
Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons camp on the east, before the tabernacle entrance—the most sacred position—guarding it for Israel.
The total of Levite males from one month old is 22,000.
Now God commands a count of Israel’s firstborn males from one month old.
The Levites will replace the firstborn, and the Levites’ cattle replace the firstborn of Israel’s cattle. “I am the LORD” underlines God’s claim.
Moses counts the firstborn as commanded.
There are 22,273 firstborn males—273 more than the number of Levites.
The Lord speaks again.
The exchange is confirmed: the Levites belong to God in place of the firstborn.
But 273 firstborn have no Levite to stand for them; they must be redeemed another way.

f.g: Bought back by paying a price.

chapters.n: Five shekels each is paid—the price set for a child in Leviticus 27. Jesus, a firstborn, was later presented in the temple according to this law.

f.g: A gerah was one-twentieth of a shekel.

chapters.n: The redemption money goes to Aaron and his sons.
Moses collects money for the surplus firstborn.
The total is 1,365 shekels (273 × 5). The idea of being bought with a price points to Christ’s redemption.

f.w: a thousand three hundred and threescore and five shekels

chapters.n: Moses gives the money to the priests, just as commanded—a careful accounting of sacred funds.
The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron about the Levites’ specific duties when the camp moves.
Count the Kohathite clan first, since they carry the holiest objects.
Only men aged thirty to fifty serve in this work—their years of greatest strength and maturity. (Numbers 8:24 gives twenty-five, perhaps including a training period.)

f.g: Here, the work force or service company.

chapters.n: The Kohathites handle “the most holy things.”
Before moving, Aaron and his sons take down the inner veil and cover the ark with it. Even the Levites were not to see the ark uncovered.

f.g: The curtain that screened the Most Holy Place.
The ark containing the covenant tablets.

chapters.n: Over the veil goes a durable leather covering, then a cloth of pure blue, and the carrying poles are inserted. The blue made the ark recognizable on the march.

f.g: Hebrew taḥash; probably fine leather, perhaps from dolphins, sea cows, or goats. The exact animal is uncertain.

chapters.n: The table of shewbread is covered with blue cloth, with its dishes and the bread still on it.
A scarlet cloth and a leather covering are added, then the poles.
The lampstand and its tools are wrapped in blue.
Everything is bundled in leather and placed on a carrying frame.
The golden incense altar is covered in blue and leather.
All the sanctuary utensils are wrapped and placed on a carrying frame.
The bronze altar of sacrifice is cleaned of ashes and covered with purple cloth.

f.g: An expensive dye, a color of royalty.

chapters.n: Its utensils go on top, covered with leather, and the poles are inserted.
Only after the priests finish covering everything may the Kohathites carry it—without touching any holy object, or they will die. Reverence for sacred things was a matter of life and death.

f.w: they shall not touch any holy thing

chapters.n: Eleazar personally oversees the lamp oil, incense, daily grain offering, anointing oil, and the whole sanctuary.
The Lord speaks again to Moses and Aaron.
Protect the Kohathites from being destroyed. Their closeness to holy things made their work dangerous.

f.g: Do not let them be destroyed.

chapters.n: Aaron and his sons must assign each Kohathite his exact task, so none approaches holy things wrongly. Clear priesthood direction protected those who served.

f.w: appoint them every one to his service

chapters.n: They must not even look at the holy things being covered. Some sacred things are veiled for a reason.
The Lord speaks to Moses about the Gershonites.
Count the Gershonites by families.
Again, men aged thirty to fifty serve.
Their work is to serve and carry loads.
They carry the tabernacle curtains, the tent coverings (including the leather outer layer), and the entrance screen.
They also carry the courtyard curtains, gate screen, and cords, and do whatever is needed with them.
Aaron and his sons direct all Gershonite work and assign their loads.
Ithamar, Aaron’s younger son, supervises the Gershonites.
Next the Merarites are counted by families.
Men aged thirty to fifty serve here as well.
The Merarites carry the heavy framework: boards, crossbars, posts, and bases.
Also the courtyard posts, bases, pegs, and ropes. Each item was assigned by name so nothing was lost.

f.g: Assign each item specifically, by name.

chapters.n: The Merarites also serve under Ithamar’s supervision.
Moses, Aaron, and the tribal leaders count the Kohathites.
Those aged thirty to fifty are counted.
There are 2,750 Kohathite workers.
This was the number fit for Kohathite service, counted as God commanded through Moses.
Next the Gershonites are counted.
Again those aged thirty to fifty.
There are 2,630 Gershonite workers.
The Gershonite count was done as the Lord commanded.
The Merarites are counted.
Those aged thirty to fifty are included.
There are 3,200 Merarite workers—the most, fitting their heavy loads.
The Merarite count is complete as commanded.
Now the total of Levites serving is given.
Those serving in ministry and carrying, aged thirty to fifty, are included.

f.w: service of the ministry, and the service of the burden
f.g: Both the work of worship and the work of carrying.

chapters.n: The total is 8,580 Levites ready to serve. “Fourscore” means eighty.
Each man was counted according to his specific service and load. Every person’s contribution was known and valued.

f.w: every one according to his service

chapters.n: With the camp organized, the Lord turns to keeping it pure, since He dwells in its center.
People with skin disease, bodily discharges, or contact with a corpse must stay outside the camp until cleansed. This was about ritual purity, and it also protected public health.
Both men and women are included. The reason: God lives in the midst of the camp.

f.w: in the midst whereof I dwell

chapters.n: Israel obeys. These separations were usually temporary, ending with the cleansing rituals of Leviticus.
A new instruction about making wrongs right.
Wronging another person is also a sin against the Lord. Our relationships with others and with God are connected.
Repentance has two parts: confessing the sin and repaying the wrong in full plus twenty percent. True repentance includes restitution whenever possible.
If the wronged person has died with no relative to receive the payment, it goes to the Lord through the priest, along with a ram for atonement.

f.g: A close relative who could act on his behalf; Hebrew go’el.

chapters.n: Sacred offerings brought to a priest belong to that priest.

f.g: Hebrew terumah, a contribution “lifted up” or set apart.

chapters.n: Each person decides what holy gifts to give, but once given to a priest, they are his.
A new law: what to do when a husband suspects his wife of unfaithfulness.
This addresses a case where a wife may have committed adultery.
The situation is secret: no witnesses and no proof. Without evidence, the case could not go to a human court.
The husband becomes jealous—whether his suspicion is true or not. The law applies in either case, protecting innocent wives from endless accusation.
He brings her to the priest with a plain barley offering—no oil or incense, since this is not a joyful offering but one that calls a possible wrong to mind.

f.g: A dry measure; a tenth of an ephah is about two quarts.
A reminder, bringing the matter before God.

chapters.n: The priest brings her before the Lord. The matter is placed in God’s hands rather than left to the angry husband.

f.g: Brought to the sanctuary for God’s judgment.

chapters.n: The priest mixes holy water with dust from the tabernacle floor in a clay pot.

f.g: Water from the sanctuary laver, perhaps.

chapters.n: He loosens her hair, places the offering in her hands, and holds the “bitter water.” The ritual was solemn and public.

f.g: Water that brings a curse if she is guilty.

chapters.n: The priest places her under oath: if innocent, the water will not harm her.

f.g: Put her under a solemn oath.

chapters.n: But if she has been unfaithful...
...the curse will affect her body. The “thigh” here is likely a polite reference to the reproductive organs; the curse may mean miscarriage or infertility.

f.g: Possibly a reference to the womb—to waste away or become infertile.

chapters.n: She answers, “Amen, amen,” accepting the oath. “Amen” means “so be it” or “truly.”
The curses are written and then washed off into the water—the words themselves dissolve into what she drinks.
She drinks the water. Physically it was harmless; only God could make it act.
The priest takes her offering, waves it before the Lord, and brings it to the altar.
A handful is burned as a memorial, and then she drinks the water.
If she is guilty, the curse takes effect and she becomes a byword among her people. God, not man, carried out the judgment.
If innocent, she is cleared and will be able to bear children. The ritual publicly vindicated a falsely accused wife.

f.g: Will be able to bear children.

chapters.n: A summary of this “law of jealousies.”
It applies whenever a husband is overcome with suspicion. Rather than taking matters into his own hands, he must bring the case before the Lord.

f.w: execute upon her all this law

chapters.n: The husband is free of guilt for bringing the matter; if the wife was unfaithful, she bears responsibility. The law placed hidden things in God’s hands, who sees all.

f.g: Bear the consequences of her sin.

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses the law of the Nazarite vow—a way any Israelite could dedicate themselves to God for a special period.
Any man or woman may take this voluntary vow. “Nazarite” comes from the Hebrew nazir, meaning “separated” or “consecrated.” It is different from “Nazarene,” meaning someone from Nazareth.

f.g: Hebrew nazir, “one separated or dedicated.” Not related to the town of Nazareth.

chapters.n: The Nazarite avoids wine, strong drink, and every grape product. Giving up an ordinary pleasure was a sign of complete devotion.

f.g: Fermented beverages other than wine, such as beer.

chapters.n: Nothing from the grapevine at all may be eaten—not even the seeds or skins.

f.g: From the seeds to the skins.

chapters.n: No razor touches the head; the hair grows long as a visible sign of the vow. Samson is the most famous Nazarite.

f.w: there shall no razor come upon his head

chapters.n: A Nazarite must avoid all dead bodies.
Not even for close family—like the high priest. The vow on his head made him especially holy.

f.w: consecration of his God is upon his head
f.g: His uncut hair was a sign of being dedicated to God.

f.w: for his father, or for his mother

chapters.n: Throughout the vow, the Nazarite is holy to the Lord. Ordinary people could choose a higher level of devotion.
If someone dies suddenly beside him, his vow is defiled. On the seventh day he shaves his head as part of cleansing.

f.w: defiled the head of his consecration

chapters.n: On the eighth day he brings two doves or young pigeons to the priest.
One is a sin offering and one a burnt offering. His head is rededicated that day.
He brings a lamb as a guilt offering and starts the vow over; the previous days do not count. A broken commitment had to be renewed from the start.
Now the rules for completing the vow successfully.
He brings three animals: a male lamb for a burnt offering, a female lamb for a sin offering, and a ram for a peace offering—all without blemish.
Also a basket of unleavened bread and cakes, plus grain and drink offerings. Completing a vow was a celebration.
The priest offers the sin offering and burnt offering before the Lord.
Then the ram as a peace offering with the bread, plus the grain and drink offerings.
The Nazarite shaves his consecrated hair at the tabernacle and burns it in the fire under the peace offering. The hair itself is given to God. Paul once joined others in completing such a vow.

f.w: shave the head of his separation

chapters.n: The priest places a boiled shoulder of the ram, a cake, and a wafer in the Nazarite’s hands.
These are waved before the Lord and given to the priest. Then the Nazarite may drink wine again—the vow is complete.

f.g: An offering presented with a forward and back motion.
The portion lifted up and given to the priest.

chapters.n: A summary: the Nazarite must keep his vow fully, and may offer more if he can afford it.

f.w: beside that that his hand shall get
f.g: In addition to whatever else he can afford.

chapters.n: The Lord speaks to Moses again, now with a blessing for the priests to give.
Aaron and his sons are taught exact words to bless Israel. Priesthood holders are authorized to pronounce God’s blessing on His people.
The famous priestly blessing begins: may the Lord bless and protect you. It is poetry in three lines, each growing longer.
May God’s face shine on you—a picture of His smile and approval—and may He show you grace.
May the Lord look upon you with favor and give you peace. “Peace” (shalom) means wholeness and well-being, not just absence of conflict.
By this blessing the priests place God’s name on Israel, marking them as His. God promises to bless them Himself. Latter-day Saints may think of taking Christ’s name upon them.
This flashback returns to the day the tabernacle was first set up and anointed—about a month before the census of chapter 1. It is the longest chapter in the Pentateuch.

f.g: Made holy, set apart for God.

chapters.n: The twelve tribal leaders—the same men who helped with the census—bring gifts.
Their first gift is practical: six covered wagons and twelve oxen to carry the tabernacle—one wagon for every two leaders.
The Lord speaks to Moses about the gift.
God accepts it and directs that the wagons go to the Levites according to their work.
Moses distributes the wagons and oxen to the Levites.
The Gershonites, who carry the fabrics, get two wagons and four oxen.
The Merarites, who carry the heavy frames, get twice as many: four wagons and eight oxen, under Ithamar.
The Kohathites get none; the holiest objects had to be carried on their shoulders. Centuries later, ignoring this rule cost Uzzah his life.
The leaders also bring gifts to dedicate the altar on the day it was anointed.

f.g: Hebrew ḥanukkah—dedication; the same word gives the later festival its name.

chapters.n: The Lord directs that each leader present his offering on his own day—twelve days of dedication. Each tribe would receive its own moment of honor.
First comes Nahshon of Judah, the leading tribe in the camp and on the march.
He brings a large silver platter (about 1.5 kg) and a silver bowl (about 0.8 kg), both full of flour mixed with oil for a grain offering.

f.g: The official standard weight, roughly 11–12 grams.

chapters.n: Also a small gold dish full of incense. Incense often pictures prayer rising to God.

f.g: A small dish or ladle, here of gold.

chapters.n: A bull, a ram, and a year-old lamb are given as burnt offerings—sacrifices wholly consumed in devotion to God.
A young male goat is given for a sin offering, to cleanse and atone.
Finally, seventeen animals for peace offerings, eaten in a shared meal celebrating fellowship with God. So ends Judah’s gift.
On day two, Nethaneel of Issachar, the tribe camped beside Judah, presents his gift.
His silver platter and bowl, filled with fine flour and oil, match Judah’s exactly. No tribe tried to outdo another.
His gold dish of incense is the same weight—ten shekels, a little over 100 grams.
Issachar’s burnt offerings: one bull, one ram, one lamb in its first year.
A goat for a sin offering, as on day one.
The same peace offerings close Issachar’s gift. The repetition honors each tribe equally.
Day three belongs to Eliab of Zebulun, completing the eastern camp.
Zebulun brings the identical silver platter and bowl of grain offering.
The gold incense dish is offered again—worship and prayer from another tribe.
The three burnt offering animals represent Zebulun’s full dedication.
A goat atones for sin on Zebulun’s behalf.
Zebulun’s peace offerings: two oxen, five rams, five male goats, five lambs.
Day four: Elizur of Reuben, leader of the southern camp, offers.
Reuben, though descended from Jacob’s firstborn, brings exactly the same silver platter and bowl as the others—no special rank here (compare Genesis 49:3-4).
The gold incense dish is presented on Reuben’s behalf.
Reuben’s bull, ram, and lamb are burnt offerings.
Reuben’s goat is the sin offering.
Reuben’s seventeen peace-offering animals complete the fourth day.
On day five Shelumiel of Simeon brings his tribe’s offering.
The silver vessels full of grain are the same as before—together they weigh 200 shekels.
Simeon’s gold dish of incense is offered.
Burnt offerings are given for Simeon.
A goat is the sin offering for Simeon.
Simeon’s peace offerings close the fifth day.
Day six: Eliasaph of Gad, son of Deuel, offers (called Reuel in Numbers 2:14).
Gad presents silver platter and bowl filled with the grain offering.
Gad’s incense in a gold dish follows.
Gad brings its three burnt-offering animals.
Gad’s sin offering goat is given.
Gad’s peace offerings finish the southern camp’s gifts.
Day seven: Elishama of Ephraim, leader of the western camp and grandfather of Joshua, offers.
Ephraim’s silver vessels match the others, full of flour and oil.
Ephraim’s golden incense dish is presented.
Ephraim’s burnt offerings are given.
Ephraim’s sin offering goat follows.
Ephraim’s peace offerings complete the seventh day.
Day eight: Gamaliel of Manasseh, Joseph’s other son’s tribe, offers.
Manasseh, though the smallest tribe in the census, gives the same as the largest. In God’s house, each tribe is equal.
Manasseh’s gold dish of incense is offered.
Manasseh’s bull, ram, and lamb are burnt offerings.
Manasseh’s goat is the sin offering.
Manasseh’s peace offerings close the eighth day.
Day nine: Abidan of Benjamin offers.
Benjamin brings the silver platter and bowl of grain offering.
Benjamin’s incense in a gold dish is presented.
Benjamin’s burnt offerings are given.
Benjamin’s sin offering goat follows.
Benjamin’s peace offerings complete the western camp’s gifts.
Day ten: Ahiezer of Dan, leader of the northern camp, offers.
Dan presents the same silver vessels full of grain.
Dan’s gold incense dish is offered.
Dan’s three burnt-offering animals are given.
Dan’s goat for a sin offering follows.
Dan’s peace offerings close the tenth day.
Day eleven: Pagiel of Asher offers.
Asher’s silver platter and bowl are presented with grain offering.
Asher’s gold dish of incense follows.
Asher’s burnt offerings are given.
Asher’s sin offering goat is presented.
Asher’s peace offerings complete the eleventh day.
Day twelve: Ahira of Naphtali, the final tribe, offers.
Naphtali brings the last silver platter and bowl.
Naphtali’s gold incense dish is the twelfth and final one.
Naphtali’s burnt offerings are given.
Naphtali’s sin offering goat is presented.
Naphtali’s peace offerings end the twelve days. The careful repetition shows that God noticed and recorded every tribe’s gift individually.

f.w: this was the offering of Ahira

chapters.n: Now the totals: twelve silver platters, twelve silver bowls, and twelve gold dishes dedicated the altar.
Total silver: 2,400 shekels—roughly 27 kilograms.
Total gold: 120 shekels—a little over a kilogram—in twelve dishes of incense.
Burnt offerings: 12 bulls, 12 rams, 12 lambs; sin offerings: 12 goats.
Peace offerings: 24 bulls, 60 rams, 60 goats, 60 lambs—enough for great celebration meals.
The chapter ends with God’s greatest gift in return: when Moses enters the tabernacle, he hears the Lord’s voice speaking from above the mercy seat between the cherubim, just as promised.

f.g: Winged figures of gold on the ark’s lid; the KJV adds an extra English plural to the Hebrew plural -im.

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses a brief instruction about the sanctuary lamps before turning to the Levites’ consecration.
When Aaron lights the seven lamps, they are to shine forward, lighting the area in front of the lampstand—toward the table of shewbread.
Aaron obeys exactly. Even small details of worship were done as God directed.
The lampstand was hammered from a single piece of gold, with flower-shaped decorations, following the pattern God showed Moses on the mount.

f.g: Gold hammered into shape rather than cast.

chapters.n: The Lord now speaks about preparing the Levites for service.
The Levites must be taken from among Israel and cleansed. Those who serve in holy places must be clean.
They are sprinkled with purifying water, shave their whole bodies, and wash their clothes—a complete fresh start.

f.g: Water for cleansing from sin or impurity.

chapters.n: They bring two young bulls: one for a burnt offering with its grain offering, and one for a sin offering.
The whole congregation gathers at the tabernacle to witness the Levites’ dedication.
The people lay their hands on the Levites, showing that the Levites represent them before God—in place of their own firstborn.

f.w: put their hands upon the Levites
f.g: A gesture of identification and transfer.

chapters.n: Aaron presents the Levites as a living “wave offering” from Israel to the Lord. The people offer the Levites, and the Levites offer their lives in service.

f.g: Literally “wave the Levites,” presenting them as a wave offering.

chapters.n: The Levites lay hands on the bulls, which are then sacrificed to make atonement for them.
The Levites are presented before Aaron and his sons, under whose direction they will serve.
This sets the Levites apart from the other tribes as God’s own.
Only after cleansing and dedication may they begin their tabernacle service.
They are entirely given to God in place of every firstborn son of Israel.
God’s claim on the firstborn goes back to the Passover in Egypt, when He spared Israel’s firstborn.

f.w: on the day that I smote every firstborn

chapters.n: The Levites stand in for all of Israel’s firstborn.
God gives the Levites to Aaron as a gift, to serve and to help protect Israel from plague when they approach the sanctuary. Their service shielded the people.
Moses, Aaron, and all the people carry out God’s instructions for the Levites.
The Levites are purified and dedicated, and Aaron makes atonement for them.
Then they begin serving in the tabernacle under Aaron and his sons, just as commanded.
The Lord gives one more instruction about the Levites’ service.
Levites begin service at age twenty-five. Chapter 4 mentions thirty for the carrying work; the difference may reflect training years or different tasks.
At fifty they retire from the heavy labor.
But retired Levites still help their brothers by guarding and assisting. Experienced servants remain valuable even when they can no longer do heavy work.

f.g: Stand guard and assist with responsibilities.

chapters.n: Another flashback: this is the first month of the second year, before the census of chapter 1. Israel prepares to keep its first Passover since leaving Egypt.

f.w: first month of the second year

chapters.n: God commands Israel to keep the Passover at its appointed time, remembering their deliverance.
It is kept at twilight on the fourteenth day, following every rite God gave.
Moses tells the people to keep the Passover.
Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai exactly as commanded—a remembrance of the lamb whose blood saved them.
A problem arises: some men had touched a dead body and were ritually unclean, so they could not take part. They bring their concern to Moses and Aaron.
They ask, sincerely, why they must be excluded from worship. Their desire to participate is touching.
Moses does not guess; he tells them to wait while he asks the Lord. A good model for leaders facing new questions.

f.w: I will hear what the LORD will command

chapters.n: The Lord answers Moses.
Those who are unclean from a corpse or traveling far away may still keep the Passover. God made room for those with valid reasons.
They keep it one month later, on the fourteenth of the second month, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. This “second Passover” showed God’s mercy.

f.g: Recalling the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.

chapters.n: All the usual rules apply: nothing left until morning and no bone broken. John saw this fulfilled in Jesus, whose bones were not broken on the cross.

f.w: nor break any bone of it

chapters.n: But anyone who is clean and at home and simply chooses not to keep the Passover is cut off. Neglecting a sacred covenant ordinance is serious.
Foreigners living among Israel may also keep the Passover by the same rules. One law for both. (Exodus 12:48 adds that males must first be circumcised.)
From the day the tabernacle was set up, a cloud covered it; at night it looked like fire. This was the visible sign of God’s presence.
The cloud by day and fire by night were constant. Isaiah later prophesied this protection over Zion in the last days.

f.w: the cloud covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night

chapters.n: When the cloud lifted, Israel moved; where it settled, they camped. God Himself led the way.
They traveled and camped at the Lord’s command. As long as the cloud stayed, they stayed.

f.w: At the commandment of the LORD
f.g: Literally “at the mouth of the LORD.”

chapters.n: Sometimes the cloud stayed many days, and Israel waited patiently. Following God includes knowing when to wait.

f.w: kept the charge of the LORD

chapters.n: Sometimes the cloud stayed only a few days. Either way, Israel followed.
Sometimes it stayed only overnight. Day or night, when it lifted, they moved. Discipleship requires readiness.
Two days, a month, or a year—the timing was God’s, not theirs.

f.g: Hebrew yamim, “days,” perhaps meaning a longer period.

chapters.n: The summary repeats “at the commandment of the LORD” three times, emphasizing complete dependence on God’s direction, given through His prophet Moses.
The Lord gives Moses final preparations before Israel leaves Sinai.
Two silver trumpets, each hammered from one piece, are made to call the people together and signal when to march. With over half a million men, clear signals were essential.

f.g: Long, straight metal trumpets, different from the ram’s-horn shofar.
Hammered from a single piece of silver.

chapters.n: When both trumpets blow, the whole community gathers at the tabernacle entrance.
A single trumpet summons only the tribal leaders.
A special signal—an “alarm,” a series of short blasts—tells the eastern camps (Judah’s group) to march.

f.g: Hebrew teru‘ah, a loud, broken blast or shout.

chapters.n: A second alarm signals the southern camps (Reuben’s group) to set out.
Gathering the people uses a long, steady blast, not the alarm. Different sounds carried different messages.

f.w: ye shall not sound an alarm

chapters.n: Only the priests blow the trumpets—a permanent ordinance. The call to gather or move came through God’s authorized servants.
In war, sounding the alarm would bring Israel to God’s remembrance, and He would save them. The trumpet was a kind of prayer for help.

f.w: ye shall be remembered before the LORD

chapters.n: Trumpets also sound over offerings on festivals and new moons, as a joyful reminder before God. Scripture often links trumpets with God’s great gatherings and the Second Coming.
On the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud lifts. After about eleven months at Sinai, Israel moves on.
They travel in stages until the cloud settles in the wilderness of Paran, a desert region south of Canaan.

f.g: A large desert area in the northeastern Sinai Peninsula.

chapters.n: This first march is carried out at the Lord’s command through Moses.
Judah’s banner leads the way under Nahshon, just as arranged in chapter 2.
Issachar marches with Judah under Nethaneel.
Zebulun follows under Eliab, completing the first division.
The tabernacle is taken down, and the Gershonites and Merarites carry its structure ahead, so it could be set up before the holy furnishings arrive.
Reuben’s division follows under Elizur.

f.w: the standard of the camp of Reuben

chapters.n: Simeon marches with Reuben under Shelumiel.
Gad follows under Eliasaph.
The Kohathites carry the holy furnishings in the middle. By the time they arrive, the others have the tabernacle standing ready to receive them.

f.g: Before they arrived; in readiness for their coming.

chapters.n: Ephraim’s division sets out under Elishama.

f.w: the standard of the camp of the children of Ephraim

chapters.n: Manasseh marches with Ephraim under Gamaliel.
Benjamin follows under Abidan.
Dan’s division forms the rear guard under Ahiezer, protecting the whole column.
Asher marches with Dan under Pagiel.
Naphtali brings up the rear under Ahira.
This was Israel’s marching order. The organization of chapter 2 is now put into action.
Moses invites Hobab, his brother-in-law from Midian, to come along and share in God’s promised blessings. (Raguel, also called Reuel and Jethro, was Moses’s father-in-law.)

f.g: Son of Raguel; called Moses’s father-in-law in Judges 4:11, perhaps because the Hebrew word can mean any in-law.
Same as Reuel, also called Jethro, the priest of Midian.

chapters.n: Hobab first declines, preferring to return to his own people.
Moses presses him: Hobab knows the desert and could be their “eyes,” guiding them to good campsites. God leads, but He also works through people’s skills.
Moses promises to share with Hobab whatever good God gives Israel. Judges 1:16 suggests his descendants did join Israel.

f.w: what goodness the LORD shall do unto us

chapters.n: Israel travels three days from Sinai, “the mount of the LORD,” with the ark of the covenant going ahead to find them a resting place.

f.w: to search out a resting place

chapters.n: The cloud of the Lord covers them by day as they travel—shade and guidance in the desert.
When the ark sets out, Moses prays, “Rise up, LORD, and let thine enemies be scattered.” This became a battle hymn of faith, echoed in Psalm 68.
When it stops, he prays, “Return, O LORD, unto the many thousands of Israel”—asking God to dwell among His people at rest.
Only three days after leaving Sinai, the people begin complaining. The Lord hears, and fire breaks out at the edges of the camp. The orderly march of chapter 10 turns quickly to grumbling.
The people cry to Moses; he prays, and the fire stops. Moses repeatedly stands between the people and judgment—a type of Christ the intercessor.

f.w: when Moses prayed unto the LORD

chapters.n: The place is named Taberah, meaning “burning.”
The “mixed multitude”—non-Israelites who came out of Egypt with them—start craving, and Israel joins in, weeping for meat. Bad attitudes spread.

f.g: A mix of people from other nations who left Egypt with Israel.

chapters.n: They remember Egypt’s free fish and fresh vegetables—forgetting the slavery. Nostalgia can make the past look better than it was.
“Our soul is dried away”—they feel their appetite has withered, with “nothing but manna” to look at. They despise the daily miracle that kept them alive.
The narrator describes manna to show how good it really was: small like coriander seed, with a pale, resin-like color.

f.g: A small round seed used as a spice.
A pale, aromatic resin, or possibly a pearl-like stone.

chapters.n: It could be ground, pounded, boiled, or baked into cakes, and tasted like something made with fresh olive oil. It was versatile and nourishing.
Manna fell with the dew each night—God’s faithful daily provision.
Every family weeps at their tent doors. God is very angry, and Moses is troubled too.

f.w: in the door of his tent

chapters.n: Moses pours out his frustration honestly to God: why have You given me such a heavy load? Scripture records even great prophets’ struggles.
Did I give birth to these people? Why must I carry them like a nursing parent carries an infant? Moses uses tender parent imagery—God is the true Father who carries Israel.

f.g: A foster parent or guardian who cares for a child.

chapters.n: Where could I get meat for all these people?
I cannot carry them all alone—the load is too heavy. Jethro had warned of this same danger.

f.w: I am not able to bear all this people alone

chapters.n: Moses even asks God to end his life rather than continue like this. Elijah and Jonah later prayed similarly in despair.
God responds with help, not rebuke: gather seventy respected elders to share the work.
God will put some of the Spirit that is on Moses onto them, so they can carry the burden with him. Shared leadership is God’s pattern; Latter-day Saints see it in quorums and councils today.

f.w: I will take of the spirit which is upon thee

chapters.n: God also answers the people: prepare yourselves, for tomorrow you will eat meat. Their complaint that life was better in Egypt reached God’s ears.
Not just for a day or two...
...but for a whole month, until it makes them sick. Their real sin was rejecting the Lord, who was living among them.

f.w: despised the LORD which is among you

chapters.n: Moses doubts: there are 600,000 men on foot—how can there be meat for a month?
Even if every animal were killed or every fish caught, would it be enough? Moses’s faith wavers under pressure.
God replies, “Is the LORD’s hand waxed short?”—Is My power limited? You will see whether My word comes true.

f.w: Is the LORD's hand waxed short?
f.g: Has the Lord’s power become weak?

chapters.n: Moses tells the people God’s words and gathers the seventy elders around the tabernacle.
The Lord descends in the cloud and places the Spirit on the elders. They prophesy—but only that once, as a sign of their calling.

f.w: they prophesied, and did not cease
f.g: The Hebrew more likely means “but did not do so again.”

chapters.n: Two of the chosen elders, Eldad and Medad, stayed in camp, yet the Spirit came on them there and they prophesied. God’s Spirit is not limited to one place.

f.w: they were of them that were written
f.g: They were on the list of the seventy.

chapters.n: A young man runs to tell Moses.
Joshua, Moses’s loyal assistant since his youth, urges Moses to stop them—protective of Moses’s authority.

Moses replies beautifully: “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish all the Lord’s people were prophets!” Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled as all may receive the Holy Ghost and the testimony of Jesus.

f.w: would God that all the LORD's people were prophets

chapters.n: Moses and the elders return to the camp.
A wind from the Lord drives quail from the sea and drops them around the camp for miles, about three feet deep. Quail migrating over Sinai still sometimes land exhausted.

f.g: About three feet (one meter); possibly the height they flew above the ground.

chapters.n: The people gather nonstop for two days and a night; even the least gathered about ten homers—a huge amount. They spread them out to dry.

f.g: A large dry measure; ten homers could be over a ton.

chapters.n: While the meat is still in their mouths, a severe plague strikes. Their greed revealed their hearts and brought judgment.

f.w: the wrath of the LORD was kindled

chapters.n: The place is named Kibroth-hattaavah, “graves of craving,” because those who lusted were buried there.
Israel moves on to Hazeroth and camps there.

f.g: A desert camping place; the name means “enclosures.”

chapters.n: Now the challenge comes from Moses’s own family. His sister Miriam (named first, likely the leader here) and brother Aaron criticize him over his “Ethiopian” (Cushite) wife.

f.g: Hebrew Cushite, from Cush (south of Egypt). She may be Zipporah or a second wife; scholars differ.

chapters.n: The real issue surfaces: jealousy over authority. “Has the Lord spoken only through Moses? Hasn’t He spoken through us too?” The Lord hears.

f.w: Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses?

chapters.n: A narrator’s note: Moses was the meekest man on earth. Meekness is strength under God’s control—Moses does not defend himself, so God defends him.
The Lord suddenly summons all three siblings to the tabernacle.
The Lord comes down in the cloud at the entrance and calls Aaron and Miriam forward.
God explains: with ordinary prophets He communicates through visions and dreams.
But Moses is different—faithful over God’s entire household.

God speaks with Moses “mouth to mouth,” clearly and not in riddles, and Moses sees the Lord’s form. Why, then, were they not afraid to criticize him? Latter-day scripture describes Moses seeing God face to face.
God’s anger burns against them, and He leaves.
As the cloud lifts, Miriam is covered with a skin disease, white like snow. Aaron is horrified.
Aaron pleads with Moses, calling him “my lord,” confessing they acted foolishly and sinned. Humility returns quickly.
Aaron begs that Miriam not be like a stillborn child whose flesh is half wasted away. It is a vivid image of her condition.
Moses, the one wronged, immediately prays for his sister: “Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee.” His short, urgent prayer shows love and forgiveness.
God agrees but requires a seven-day period of shame outside the camp, as a father’s public rebuke would bring. Then she may return.

f.g: A sign of strong public disapproval.

chapters.n: Miriam spends seven days outside the camp, and the whole nation waits for her. Her place among the people was honored even in discipline.

f.w: the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again

chapters.n: Afterward Israel leaves Hazeroth and camps in the wilderness of Paran, near Canaan’s southern border.
From the wilderness of Paran, close to Canaan, the Lord speaks to Moses about scouting the land. Deuteronomy 1:22 adds that the people first requested it.
Send twelve men, a leader from each tribe, to explore Canaan—the land God is already giving them.

f.w: which I give unto the children of Israel

chapters.n: Moses sends them, all respected leaders—though different men from the tribal chiefs of chapter 1.
From Reuben: Shammua son of Zaccur.
From Simeon: Shaphat son of Hori.
From Judah: Caleb son of Jephunneh, who will become a hero of faith in this story.
From Issachar: Igal son of Joseph.
From Ephraim: Oshea (Hoshea) son of Nun—better known as Joshua.
From Benjamin: Palti son of Raphu.
From Zebulun: Gaddiel son of Sodi.
From Manasseh (one of Joseph’s two tribes): Gaddi son of Susi.
From Dan: Ammiel son of Gemalli.
From Asher: Sethur son of Michael.
From Naphtali: Nahbi son of Vophsi.
From Gad: Geuel son of Machi. Of these twelve names, only Caleb and Joshua are remembered for faith.
Moses renames Hoshea as Jehoshua (Joshua), “Jehovah is salvation.” Jesus is the Greek form of this same name.

f.g: Hebrew Yehoshua, “Jehovah saves”; in Greek, Iēsous (Jesus).

chapters.n: Moses sends them north through the Negev (the dry south) and into the hill country.

f.g: Hebrew negev, the dry southern region of Canaan.

chapters.n: Their mission: learn about the land and its people—strong or weak, few or many.
Is the land good? Are the cities open camps or fortified?
Is the soil rich? Are there trees? Be courageous and bring back fruit. It was the season of first-ripe grapes, around late summer.
They explore from the wilderness of Zin in the south to Rehob near Hamath in the far north—the full length of the land.

f.g: Desert area on Canaan’s southern border.
A city in Syria; “the entrance of Hamath” marked Israel’s ideal northern border.

chapters.n: At Hebron they see the descendants of Anak, a people known for great size. Hebron was ancient—built seven years before Zoan in Egypt—and was where Abraham was buried.

f.g: The Anakim, a clan famed for their height.
Tanis, a city in Egypt’s delta.

chapters.n: At the Eshcol valley they cut a grape cluster so large two men carried it on a pole, plus pomegranates and figs. The land was truly abundant.

f.w: bare it between two upon a staff
f.g: Carried it on a pole between two men.

chapters.n: The valley was named Eshcol, meaning “cluster.”
They return after forty days. Forty will soon become an important number in Israel’s story.
They report to Moses, Aaron, and everyone at Kadesh in Paran, showing the fruit.

f.g: Kadesh-barnea, an oasis that became Israel’s base in the wilderness.

chapters.n: Their report starts well: the land does flow with milk and honey—just as God promised. Here is the proof.
“Nevertheless”—the turning word. The people are strong, the cities walled, and the Anakim are there. They see the obstacles more than the promise.
They list the nations: Amalekites in the south, Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites in the hills, and Canaanites along the coast and Jordan.
Caleb quiets the crowd: “Let us go up at once and take it—we can certainly do it!” He trusts God’s promise over appearances.

f.w: we are well able to overcome it

chapters.n: But the other spies (except Joshua) say, “We can’t—they are stronger than we are.” They leave God out of the equation.
They spread a bad report: the land “eats up its inhabitants”—perhaps meaning it is constantly fought over—and the people are huge. Fear exaggerates.

f.g: Devours those who live there—perhaps through warfare or hardship.

chapters.n: “We saw the giants... and we were like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and so we were in theirs.” How they saw themselves shaped how they thought others saw them. Faith would have measured the giants against God instead.

f.g: Hebrew nephilim, an ancient term for people of great size.

chapters.n: After the spies’ frightening report, the whole community cries and weeps all night. Fear spreads like a fire through the camp.
They complain against Moses and Aaron: “We wish we had died in Egypt or in this desert!” They will get the second half of that wish.
They accuse God of bringing them to die by the sword and leaving their families as victims. Shouldn’t we go back to Egypt?
They even propose choosing a new leader to take them back to slavery. It is a complete rejection of God’s deliverance.
Moses and Aaron fall face down before everyone—an act of humility and urgent pleading before God.
Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes in grief at the people’s rebellion.

f.g: Tore their garments, a sign of deep distress.

chapters.n: They insist: the land is exceedingly good.
If the Lord is pleased with us, He will bring us in and give it to us. Success depends on God, not on our strength.

f.w: If the LORD delight in us

chapters.n: Do not rebel or fear. The Canaanites are “bread for us”—we will swallow them up. Their protection is gone, but the Lord is with us.
The crowd threatens to stone Joshua and Caleb. At that moment the Lord’s glory appears at the tabernacle for all to see.

f.w: the glory of the LORD appeared

chapters.n: The Lord asks: How long will these people despise Me? How long until they trust Me, after all the miracles they have seen?
God proposes destroying them and making a greater nation from Moses—the same offer as after the golden calf. Will Moses accept?

f.w: make of thee a greater nation

chapters.n: Moses refuses and intercedes. His first argument: the Egyptians will hear about it...
...and tell the Canaanites, who already know that You are with this people, seen face to face, leading them by cloud and fire.
If You kill them all at once, the nations who heard of Your fame will talk...
...saying the Lord could not bring His people into the land, so He killed them. Moses cares more for God’s honor than his own advancement.
Moses’s second argument: show Your great power—not in destroying, but in forgiving, as You Yourself have said.

f.w: let the power of my Lord be great
f.g: Show the greatness of Your power.

chapters.n: He quotes God’s own description of Himself: patient, full of mercy, forgiving, yet just. Moses pleads with God using God’s own words.

f.w: The LORD is longsuffering, and of great mercy

chapters.n: “Pardon this people according to Your great mercy, as You have forgiven them from Egypt until now.” A model of intercessory prayer.
The Lord answers: “I have pardoned, as you asked.” Moses’s prayer prevails. The nation is spared.

f.w: I have pardoned according to thy word

chapters.n: But God swears that His glory will fill the whole earth—His purposes will not fail even when people do.

f.w: all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD

chapters.n: Those who saw His miracles yet tested Him “ten times”—a way of saying “over and over”—and would not listen...
...will not see the promised land. Forgiveness spared the nation, but consequences remained for those who rejected God.

f.w: they shall not see the land

chapters.n: Caleb is the exception: he “had another spirit” and “followed me fully.” He will enter the land, and his children will inherit it.
Since enemies occupy the valleys, Israel must turn back tomorrow toward the Red Sea, away from Canaan.

f.g: Here probably the Gulf of Aqaba, an arm of the Red Sea.

chapters.n: The Lord speaks again to Moses and Aaron, announcing the formal sentence.
How long must I put up with this wicked community’s complaining? I have heard all of it.
“As you have spoken in My ears, so will I do to you.” Their own words become their judgment.

f.w: as ye have spoken in mine ears

chapters.n: Their bodies will fall in this wilderness—every man counted in the census, twenty and older, who complained.

f.w: from twenty years old and upward

chapters.n: None will enter the promised land except Caleb and Joshua.
But their children, whom they said would become victims, God will bring in. The very ones they feared for will receive the promise.
As for the faithless adults, they will die in the wilderness.
Their children will wander forty years as shepherds, suffering for their parents’ unfaithfulness until that generation has passed.

f.g: Suffer the consequences of your unfaithfulness.

chapters.n: One year for each day the spies explored—forty years. They will learn what it means to have God against them.

f.g: My opposition; what it is like when I turn against you.

chapters.n: God declares that He will surely do this; that generation will die in the wilderness.
The spies who caused the people to rebel by slandering the land...
...die immediately by a plague before the Lord. Leaders who mislead others bear greater responsibility.
Only Joshua and Caleb survive out of the twelve spies. Faith preserved them.
Moses tells everyone the Lord’s words, and the people mourn deeply.
Early next morning they decide to attack after all: “We have sinned—now we will go up!” But obedience after the fact is not the same as repentance.
Moses warns: why are you disobeying again? It will not succeed.
Do not go, because the Lord is not with you. You will be defeated.

f.w: the LORD is not among you

chapters.n: The Amalekites and Canaanites will defeat you, because you turned away from the Lord, so He will not be with you.
They presumed to go up anyway, but the ark and Moses stayed in camp. Going without God’s presence is presumption, not faith.

The Amalekites and Canaanites came down from the hills and routed them as far as Hormah. The tragic chapter shows the cost of unbelief—first refusing to go when God said go, then going when He said stop.

f.g: A town in southern Canaan; the name relates to “destruction.”

chapters.n: A new set of instructions begins. Coming right after the failure at Kadesh in chapter 14, these laws quietly promise that Israel will still reach the land, even though that generation will not.
The Lord speaks of “when,” not “if.” Despite the people’s rebellion, His promise of a homeland stands, and the next generation will offer these sacrifices there.

f.g: The land where they will settle and live — Canaan.

chapters.n: These rules apply to voluntary and festival offerings of cattle or sheep. “Sweet savour” pictures God being pleased with sincere worship, as a pleasant smell rising from the altar.

f.g: A gift given simply out of a willing heart, not because it was required.

chapters.n: Every animal sacrifice was to be joined by a grain offering of flour and oil. Bread, oil, and life together acknowledged that all of Israel’s food came from God.

f.g: In KJV English “meat” means food in general; this is a grain (flour) offering.
A tenth of an ephah — roughly two to four pounds of flour.
A liquid measure, perhaps about a gallon (scholars’ estimates vary).

chapters.n: Wine was also poured out as a drink offering with each lamb. A small, joyful touch: the produce of vineyards Israel did not yet own is already part of the plan.

f.g: Wine poured out beside the altar as a gift to God.

chapters.n: A larger animal called for a larger grain offering. The amounts grow with the size of the sacrifice, keeping the whole offering in proportion.
With a ram, the wine offering also increases to a third of a hin. The detail shows that worship was meant to be orderly and complete.
Now the rules turn to the largest offering, a young bull, whether given as a burnt offering, to fulfill a vow, or as a peace offering shared in fellowship.
A bull required three tenths of flour mixed with half a hin of oil — the biggest grain offering of the set.
Half a hin of wine accompanied the bull. Together the animal, grain, oil, and wine formed one complete gift that pleased the Lord.
This verse sums up the scale: bull, ram, lamb, or young goat, each had its matching portions.
If a person brought several animals, each one needed its own grain and drink offering. Nothing was to be done halfway.
Native-born Israelites were to follow this pattern every time they offered a sacrifice by fire.
Foreigners living among Israel who wished to worship the Lord were welcome to do so, following the same pattern as everyone else.

f.g: A resident foreigner — someone not born an Israelite but living in their community.

chapters.n: A striking principle of equality: before the Lord the outsider and the Israelite stand alike. God’s covenant has always reached beyond one family line.

f.w: as ye are, so shall the stranger be

chapters.n: One law for all. The repetition stresses that God does not keep two standards, one for insiders and one for newcomers.
A second set of instructions begins, again looking ahead to life in the promised land.
Again the Lord speaks confidently: He is the one bringing Israel into the land.
When Israel first eats the bread grown in Canaan, they are to set some apart for the Lord. The first portion belongs to the Giver.

f.g: A portion “lifted up” or set apart from the rest and given to the Lord (and His priests).

chapters.n: A cake from the first batch of dough is given to the Lord, just as the first grain from the threshing floor was. It is a way of saying “thank you” before eating.

f.g: A flat, hard place where harvested grain was beaten to separate the kernels from the husks.

chapters.n: This is to be a lasting practice. Giving God the first, rather than the leftovers, teaches gratitude in everyday life.
Now the Lord addresses failure. What happens when Israel unintentionally falls short of His commandments?

f.g: Gone astray or made a mistake without meaning to.

chapters.n: This covers any of the commandments given through Moses, from the beginning onward. God expected that His people would sometimes slip.
If the whole community sins without realizing it, they offer a bull as a burnt offering and a goat as a sin offering together. There is a remedy for collective mistakes.

f.g: Here, sin done unintentionally or without knowing it.

chapters.n: Through the priest’s atonement the people are forgiven. These sacrifices pointed forward to Jesus Christ, whose Atonement truly covers sins committed in ignorance.
Forgiveness reaches the whole congregation — including the foreigners living among them.
An individual who sins unintentionally brings a year-old female goat as a sin offering.

f.w: she goat of the first year

chapters.n: The priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven. God does not leave honest mistakes unresolved; He provides a way back.
Again, the same merciful law applies to Israelite and stranger alike.
Deliberate, defiant sin is different. To sin “presumptuously” is to sin with a raised fist, knowing better. Such a person insults the Lord and is cut off from the people.

f.g: Hebrew “with a high hand” — openly, defiantly, on purpose.
Removed from the covenant community; sometimes this meant death.

chapters.n: The reason: such a person has despised God’s word itself. The guilt rests on them alone. The contrast teaches that God weighs our intentions, not just our acts.

f.w: despised the word of the LORD

chapters.n: A real example follows: a man was caught gathering firewood on the Sabbath. Coming right after the law on defiant sin, the story seems meant to illustrate it.
Those who found him brought him to Moses, Aaron, and the community, rather than taking matters into their own hands.
They held him in custody because the penalty had not yet been made clear. Moses waited for the Lord’s direction instead of guessing.

f.g: in ward = under guard, in custody

chapters.n: The Lord declared the death penalty. To modern readers this is very hard; in Israel’s setting the Sabbath was a sign of the covenant itself, and open defiance of it threatened the whole people’s bond with God.

f.g: Outside the camp, keeping the community’s holy space undefiled.

chapters.n: The sentence was carried out as the Lord commanded. The story shows how seriously the covenant of the Sabbath was taken at that time.
A gentler instruction closes the chapter, given as a lasting help to remember.
Israelites were to wear tassels on the corners of their clothes, each with a blue cord. Blue was a costly, royal color, reminding them that they belonged to a holy King.

f.g: Tassels on the corners of a garment (Hebrew tsitsit), still worn by many Jews today.
ribband = ribbon; a blue (or violet) cord.

f.w: fringes in the borders of their garments

chapters.n: The tassels were a visual reminder: every glance would recall God’s commandments and help them resist following every desire of their hearts and eyes into spiritual unfaithfulness.

f.g: A strong biblical image for unfaithfulness to God, especially idolatry, compared to betraying a marriage.

chapters.n: The purpose of remembering is doing — and becoming holy. Latter-day Saints may think of the sacrament prayers, where we promise to “always remember him.”
The chapter closes with God’s signature: “I am the LORD your God,” who freed them from Egypt. Every law rests on that relationship and that rescue.

f.g: Small capitals render the divine name YHWH (Jehovah), whom Latter-day Saints understand to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

chapters.n: A rebellion forms. Korah is a Levite, a cousin of Moses and Aaron through Kohath; Dathan, Abiram, and On come from Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn. Both groups may have felt passed over for leadership.

f.g: The Levite clan that carried the holiest furnishings of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:4-15).

chapters.n: They are joined by 250 well-known community leaders. This was not a fringe protest but a serious challenge from respected men.

f.g: Chiefs or leaders chosen from the congregation.

chapters.n: Their argument sounds spiritual: everyone is holy, so why should Moses and Aaron be above anyone else? But they twist a true idea (Israel is a holy people) into a denial that God calls specific leaders.

f.w: Ye take too much upon you
f.g: “You have gone too far” — you claim more authority than you should.

chapters.n: Moses’ first response is not anger but humility: he falls on his face before God.
Moses refuses to settle the matter himself. Tomorrow the Lord will show whom He has chosen. Priesthood authority comes from God’s call, not human campaign.
Moses proposes a test: Korah’s group should bring censers, the pans used to burn incense in priestly worship.

f.g: Metal fire-pans for carrying hot coals and burning incense — a duty reserved for priests.

chapters.n: Offering incense was the work of priests. Whoever the Lord accepts will be shown to be holy. Moses turns their own words back on them: “Ye take too much upon you.”
Moses now speaks directly to Korah and his fellow Levites.
Is it not enough, Moses asks, that God already set the Levites apart to serve at His tabernacle? They had a sacred calling but were not content with it.

f.w: Seemeth it but a small thing unto you
f.g: “Does it seem a small thing to you?”

chapters.n: Here is the real issue: Korah wants the priesthood office given to Aaron’s family. Latter-day Saints may recognize the difference between callings and offices — each has its place.
Rebelling against God’s chosen servants is really rebelling against God. Aaron is only a servant; their complaint is against the One who called him.

f.g: Grumble or complain, especially in rebellion.

chapters.n: Moses summons Dathan and Abiram, but they flatly refuse to come.

f.g: Likely to come before Moses at the tabernacle; the refusal itself is defiance.

chapters.n: Their complaint stuns: they call Egypt — the land of slavery — a land of milk and honey! They accuse Moses of dragging them out to die so he can rule them.

f.g: A phrase God used for Canaan; they reapply it to Egypt, turning God’s promise upside down.

chapters.n: They mock Moses for failing to deliver the promised land — forgetting it was their own unbelief that delayed it. “Put out the eyes” likely means “Do you think you can blind these men to the truth?”

f.w: wilt thou put out the eyes of these men?
f.g: An idiom: “Will you fool these men?” or “Will you treat us as blind?”

chapters.n: Moses is deeply angry and asks God not to accept their offering. He defends his honesty: he never took so much as a donkey from them.

f.w: I have not taken one ass from them

chapters.n: Moses repeats the challenge: Korah, his followers, and Aaron must all appear before the Lord tomorrow.
Each of the 250 men, Korah, and Aaron is to bring a censer with incense. Side by side, God will make His choice plain.
The challengers came, censers lit, and stood at the tabernacle entrance alongside Moses and Aaron.

f.g: The tent of meeting, where God met with His people.

chapters.n: Korah rallies the whole congregation to his side. At that moment the glory of the Lord appears to everyone — God Himself is about to answer.
The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron.
God warns Moses and Aaron to step away, for He is about to destroy the whole assembly that sided with Korah.
Moses and Aaron plead for the people. They call God “the God of the spirits of all flesh” — the Father of every spirit — and ask Him not to punish everyone for one man’s sin.

f.w: God of the spirits of all flesh
shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation?

chapters.n: The Lord answers their intercession. Their plea for mercy changes what happens next — prayer matters.
Rather than destroying everyone, God tells the people to move away from the tents of the three ringleaders. Mercy makes room for separation.

f.g: Here “tabernacle” means the dwelling tents of these men, not the Lord’s tabernacle.

chapters.n: Moses goes personally to the tents of Dathan and Abiram — the men who refused to come to him — followed by the elders.
Moses urges everyone to separate from the rebels and touch nothing of theirs. Sin can draw in those who linger near it.
The people pull back on every side. Dathan and Abiram stand defiantly at their tent doors with their families.
Moses states the test plainly: what is about to happen will prove that he did not invent his calling. God sent him.
If these men die a normal death, then Moses is not God’s messenger.

f.w: visited after the visitation of all men
f.g: If they meet the ordinary fate everyone meets.

chapters.n: But if God does something unheard of — the earth opening to swallow them alive — everyone will know these men have provoked the Lord.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the place of the dead, pictured as deep in the earth.

chapters.n: As soon as Moses finished speaking, the ground split open beneath them.
The earth swallowed the rebels, their households, Korah’s men, and their goods. Numbers 26:11 notes that Korah’s own sons did not die — later their descendants wrote several Psalms.
They went down alive into the pit, and the ground closed over them. Their rebellion ended in being removed from the congregation they had tried to lead.
Terrified by the screams, the people ran, afraid the earth would swallow them too.
Then fire came from the Lord and consumed the 250 men offering incense — the very act by which they had claimed the priesthood.

f.w: there came out a fire from the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord gives instructions about what remains.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son and a priest, is to gather the censers from the ashes and scatter the coals. The censers had been offered before the Lord, so they had become holy objects.

f.g: hallowed = made holy, set apart for God
yonder = over there, at a distance

chapters.n: The bronze censers are to be hammered into a covering for the altar — a permanent reminder. The men had sinned “against their own souls”: rebellion ultimately harms the rebel most.

f.g: They forfeited their own lives through their sin.

chapters.n: Eleazar does as commanded, turning the censers into plates for the altar.
Every time Israel saw the altar, they would remember: only those called through Aaron’s line could offer incense. Authority must be given by God.

f.g: Here, anyone outside Aaron’s priestly family, even an Israelite.

f.w: that no stranger, which is not of the seed of Aaron, come near to offer incense

chapters.n: Astonishingly, the very next day the whole community blames Moses and Aaron for the deaths. Hearts hardened by murmuring rarely learn quickly.

f.g: on the morrow = the next day

chapters.n: As the crowd gathers against them, the cloud covers the tabernacle and God’s glory appears again.
Moses and Aaron go to the front of the tabernacle.
Once more the Lord speaks to Moses, this time about the crowd that has turned against him.
Again God warns that He will destroy the people, and again Moses and Aaron fall to the ground — interceding rather than fleeing.
Moses acts quickly: Aaron must take fire from the altar, add incense, and rush into the crowd to make atonement, because a plague has started.

f.g: Here the incense represents prayer and intercession that turns away judgment.

chapters.n: Aaron runs into the midst of the dying people — the same people who had just accused him — offering incense on their behalf.
Aaron stands between the dead and the living, and the plague stops. It is a powerful picture of Jesus Christ, the great High Priest, who stands between us and death.

f.w: he stood between the dead and the living

chapters.n: Some 14,700 died in the plague, in addition to those who died with Korah. The numbers underline the cost of spreading rebellion.
Aaron returns to Moses at the tabernacle, and the plague has ended. His humble intercession — not Korah’s ambition — showed who truly held the priesthood.
After Korah’s rebellion and the plague, the Lord gives a gentle, unmistakable sign to settle who holds the priesthood once and for all.
Each tribal leader is to bring a staff — a walking stick that also symbolized authority — with his name written on it. Twelve tribes, twelve rods.

f.g: A staff; in Hebrew the same word (matteh) also means “tribe,” fitting for a test about tribal authority.

chapters.n: Aaron’s name goes on the rod for Levi. The question being tested: which family has God chosen to lead in priestly service?
The rods are placed in the tabernacle before the ark of the covenant, the place where God met with Moses.

f.g: The tablets of the covenant kept in the ark — so “before the testimony” means in front of the ark.

f.w: where I will meet with you

chapters.n: The rod of God’s chosen man will blossom. The aim is merciful: to end the murmuring that had already cost so many lives.

f.w: I will make to cease from me the murmurings
f.g: “I will put a stop to the grumbling that reaches me.”

chapters.n: The twelve leaders each give a rod, and Aaron’s is placed among them. Everyone has an equal chance; the outcome will be God’s alone.
Moses sets the rods before the Lord overnight.

f.g: Another name for the tabernacle, the tent containing the “testimony” (covenant tablets).

chapters.n: By morning, Aaron’s dead stick has budded, flowered, and produced ripe almonds — all at once. Life from dead wood is a powerful sign of God’s power and approval.

f.g: The almond is the first tree to blossom in spring in Israel; its Hebrew name (shaqed) sounds like “watchful.”

chapters.n: Moses brings all the rods out for everyone to see. Each leader takes back his own unchanged stick, while Aaron’s alone is alive.
Aaron’s rod is to be kept before the ark as a lasting warning to rebels, so that the people would stop murmuring and not die. A reminder can save lives.
Moses obeys exactly as the Lord commanded, placing Aaron’s blossoming rod back before the ark.
Finally convinced, the people swing to the opposite extreme — terror. “We’re all going to die!” they cry.
They fear even approaching the tabernacle. Chapter 18 answers this fear: God provides priests and Levites to guard the holy things so the people can be safe near His presence.
Answering the people’s fear (17:12-13), the Lord speaks directly to Aaron. The priests will carry responsibility for any offense against the sanctuary, shielding the people.

f.w: bear the iniquity of the sanctuary
f.g: Take responsibility for any wrongdoing connected with the holy place and its service.

chapters.n: The rest of the tribe of Levi will assist Aaron, but only Aaron and his sons serve before the ark itself. The word “joined” plays on the name Levi, which sounds like the Hebrew for “joined.”
Levites guard and care for the tabernacle, but they must not touch the holy vessels or the altar. Boundaries protect both the Levites and the priests.
The Levites will handle all the tabernacle work, and no unauthorized person may come near.

f.g: Here, anyone not appointed to that service.

chapters.n: If the priests faithfully guard the sanctuary and altar, God’s wrath will no longer break out on Israel as it did with Korah.
God calls the Levites a gift — given to the priests to help with the work of the tabernacle. Service in God’s house is a privilege, not a burden.
The priesthood itself is called “a service of gift” — something God gives, not something a person can seize. Only priests may serve at the altar and inside the veil.

f.g: Behind the curtain separating the holy place from the most holy place.

chapters.n: Now the Lord explains how priests will be supported: they receive portions of the offerings Israel brings. “Anointing” refers to their being set apart for this work.

f.g: Because they were anointed (consecrated) as priests.
Portions set apart or “lifted up” for the Lord and given to His priests.

chapters.n: The “most holy” portions — parts of the grain, sin, and guilt offerings not burned on the altar — belong to the priests.

f.g: An offering for guilt, often involving repayment for wrong done (Leviticus 5-6).

chapters.n: These most holy portions must be eaten in a holy place, and only by the males of the priestly family.

f.g: Likely the sacred tabernacle court area, rather than the inner room itself.

chapters.n: Other offerings could be shared with the priest’s whole family, sons and daughters alike, as long as they were ritually clean.

f.g: Portions waved before the Lord as a sign of presenting them to Him.
Ritually pure, not under any temporary impurity.

chapters.n: The best of the oil, wine, and grain — the first part of each harvest — also goes to the priests.
Whatever first ripens in the land and is brought to the Lord becomes the priests’ food.
Anything permanently dedicated to the Lord belongs to the priests.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — something wholly and irrevocably given to God.

chapters.n: Every firstborn belongs to the Lord. Firstborn sons and firstborn of unclean animals (like donkeys) were to be “redeemed” — bought back — instead of sacrificed.

f.g: Opens the womb — that is, is firstborn.

chapters.n: A firstborn son was redeemed at one month old for five shekels of silver, a fixed price measured by the sanctuary’s standard weight.

f.g: A gerah was the smallest weight unit; twenty made one shekel.
