chapters.n: Firstborn calves, lambs, and kids, however, are not redeemed. They are holy and are sacrificed on the altar.
The meat from these firstborn sacrifices goes to the priests, like the breast and right shoulder of the peace offerings.
God seals this arrangement as “a covenant of salt” — salt preserves and does not decay, so the phrase means a lasting, unbreakable covenant.
A beautiful promise: Aaron will own no land in Canaan, because the Lord Himself is his portion and inheritance. Those who serve God are cared for by Him.

f.w: I am thy part and thine inheritance

chapters.n: The Levites receive Israel’s tithes — a tenth of the harvest — as their inheritance in return for their tabernacle service.
Ordinary Israelites must not approach the tabernacle in ways reserved for its ministers, so that no one bears sin and dies.
The Levites take on that sacred work and its responsibilities. Because of this calling, they receive no tribal land.
Instead of land, the tithes offered to the Lord are given to the Levites as their inheritance.

f.g: A tithe is a tenth part, given to God.

chapters.n: Now the Lord gives Moses a message for the Levites themselves.
The Levites must also pay tithing: a tenth of the tithes they receive is offered to the Lord. No one is exempt from giving.

f.w: a tenth part of the tithe
f.g: Often called “the tithe of the tithe.”

chapters.n: God counts the Levites’ tithe as if it were their own harvest from field and winepress. Their offering is just as acceptable as a farmer’s.

f.g: In KJV English “corn” means grain, such as wheat or barley.

chapters.n: The Levites’ tithe goes to Aaron the priest.
They must give from the best portion, not the leftovers. Giving God the best is a sign of real devotion.
Once they have given the best part, the rest is theirs to use like any farmer’s harvest.
Levites and their families may eat it anywhere. It is their honest wages for serving at the tabernacle.
If they give the best portion as commanded, they will be blameless. But to treat holy gifts carelessly would profane them — a warning to handle sacred things with respect.

f.g: Profane, treat as common something that is holy.

chapters.n: After so many deaths in the wilderness (chapters 14–17), the Lord gives Moses and Aaron a way for the living to be cleansed after contact with the dead.
Israel is to bring a perfect red cow that has never worn a yoke — never been used for ordinary work. Red may suggest blood and life; her unused state marks her as wholly set apart for God.

f.g: A young cow that has not yet borne a calf, reddish-brown in color.
A wooden bar fitted over an animal’s neck for pulling plows or carts.

chapters.n: Unusually, the heifer is taken outside the camp to be killed, in Eleazar’s presence. Hebrews notes that Jesus also suffered outside the city gate.

f.g: Aaron’s son, who would succeed him as high priest. Aaron himself stays clear of this defiling task.

chapters.n: Eleazar sprinkles her blood seven times toward the tabernacle, linking the sacrifice to God’s dwelling. Seven symbolizes completeness.
The whole animal — skin, flesh, blood, and dung — is burned completely. Nothing is eaten; all becomes ash for cleansing.
Cedar, hyssop, and scarlet yarn are thrown into the fire. These same three items were used to cleanse people healed of leprosy, and all three are associated with life and purification.

f.w: cedar wood, and hyssop, and scarlet

f.g: A small, bushy plant whose branches worked well for sprinkling liquids.

chapters.n: A paradox: the ashes cleanse others, yet the priest who handles the ritual becomes unclean until evening and must wash. The purifier takes on impurity — a hint of Christ, who took our sins upon Himself.

f.g: Until evening, when a new day began in Israel’s reckoning.
Ritually impure — not sinful, but temporarily unable to take part in holy worship.

chapters.n: The one who burns the heifer must also wash and remains unclean until evening.
A clean person gathers the ashes and stores them outside the camp. Mixed with water, they make the “water of separation” — a ready supply for anyone needing cleansing.

f.g: Also translated “water for impurity” — water that removes uncleanness.

chapters.n: The one gathering ashes becomes unclean until evening too. This cleansing law applies to Israelites and foreigners alike, permanently.

f.g: A lasting law for Israel’s generations.

chapters.n: Touching a dead body made a person unclean for seven days. Death was the opposite of the living God, so contact with it kept one from His sanctuary until cleansed.
The cleansing water was sprinkled on the third and seventh days. Skip the third-day step, and the person would not be clean on the seventh.

f.g: Many Christians see a hint of resurrection here, as Christ rose on the third day.

chapters.n: Refusing to be cleansed was serious: such a person brought defilement into God’s dwelling and was cut off. Ignoring God’s provided remedy is the real danger.

f.w: defileth the tabernacle of the LORD
f.g: Brings impurity into the sacred camp where God dwells.

chapters.n: When someone dies in a tent, everyone who enters and everything inside becomes unclean for seven days.
Any uncovered container in that tent becomes unclean, since impurity was thought to settle into open vessels.

f.g: A jar or pot without a sealed lid.

chapters.n: The same applies in the open: touching a battle casualty, a corpse, a human bone, or a grave brings seven days of uncleanness.
To cleanse, some of the ashes are put in a vessel with fresh, running water.

f.g: Hebrew “living water” — fresh water from a spring or stream.

chapters.n: A clean person dips hyssop in the water and sprinkles the tent, the vessels, and each defiled person.
Sprinkling happens on the third and seventh days. On the seventh, the person washes clothes, bathes, and is clean by evening.
Again, whoever refuses this cleansing is cut off, having defiled the Lord’s sanctuary. God offers purity freely, but it must be accepted.
Even the one who sprinkles the water, or who touches it, becomes unclean until evening — a reminder that holy things must be handled with care.
Uncleanness spreads by touch: anything the unclean person touches becomes unclean, and so does anyone who touches it. Spiritual impurity, too, spreads unless it is dealt with.
Many years have passed — this is likely near the end of the forty years. Back at Kadesh, Miriam, Moses’ sister and a prophetess, dies and is buried.

f.g: A wilderness region on the southern edge of Canaan, around Kadesh.

chapters.n: Once again there is no water, and the people gang up on Moses and Aaron. The new generation repeats their parents’ pattern.
They quarrel with Moses and wish they had died with those struck down earlier, perhaps referring to Korah’s rebellion.
They accuse Moses and Aaron of leading them into the desert to die along with their livestock.
Why leave Egypt for this barren place, they ask — no grain, figs, grapes, pomegranates, or water. Ironically, those are exactly the fruits the spies brought from Canaan.

f.w: figs, or of vines, or of pomegranates

chapters.n: Moses and Aaron go to the tabernacle and fall on their faces. The glory of the Lord appears to them.
The Lord answers Moses — not with anger at the people this time, but with a plan to give them water.
God tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock in front of everyone, and it will give water. Note the difference from Exodus 17, where Moses was told to strike the rock.

f.g: Likely Aaron’s budded rod kept “before the LORD” (17:10), or Moses’ own staff of miracles.

chapters.n: Moses takes the rod from before the Lord, as instructed.
Gathering the people, Moses speaks sharply: “Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water?” In anger he speaks as though he and Aaron, rather than God, provide the miracle.
Instead of speaking to the rock, Moses strikes it twice. God still graciously sends abundant water for people and animals. Paul later taught that this Rock represents Christ.
The Lord tells Moses and Aaron they will not lead Israel into the land, because they did not trust Him enough to honor Him as holy before the people. Leaders are held to a higher standard.

f.g: To treat God as holy — to show the people that the power and glory are His.

f.w: ye shall not bring this congregation into the land

chapters.n: The place is called Meribah, meaning “strife” or “quarreling.” Even so, the Lord showed Himself holy among them by providing for them.
Israel now heads toward Canaan from the east. Moses asks the king of Edom for passage, appealing to family ties — Edom descended from Esau, Jacob’s twin brother.
Moses summarizes Israel’s history: going down to Egypt and being mistreated there.
When they cried to the Lord, He heard them and sent an angel to bring them out. Now they are at Kadesh, on Edom’s border.
Israel promises to pass through carefully on the main road, touching no fields, vineyards, or wells. It is a respectful, peaceful request.

f.g: The King’s Highway, a major ancient trade route running north–south east of the Jordan and Dead Sea.

chapters.n: Edom flatly refuses and threatens to meet Israel with the sword. The brother nation shows no brotherly kindness.
Israel tries again, offering to pay even for water and to simply walk through.
Edom again refuses and comes out with a large, strong army.
Rather than fight their relatives, Israel turns away — obeying God’s later instruction not to provoke Edom.
Leaving Kadesh, the whole congregation travels to Mount Hor.

f.g: A mountain on Edom’s border; its exact location is uncertain.

chapters.n: At Mount Hor the Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron.

f.g: In KJV English, “coast” often means border or territory, not seashore.

chapters.n: Aaron is about to die. “Gathered unto his people” is a gentle way of saying he will join his ancestors in death — implying life continues beyond the grave.
Moses is to bring Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain.
Aaron’s high priestly clothing is to be transferred to Eleazar — a visible passing of the priestly office to the next generation.
Moses obeys, and the three climb the mountain with all Israel watching.
Moses puts Aaron’s robes on Eleazar, and Aaron dies on the mountaintop. Only Moses and Eleazar come down. The priesthood continues though the man passes on.
All Israel mourns Aaron for thirty days. Despite their complaints, they loved the priest who had stood between them and the plague.
The Canaanite king of Arad, in the Negev desert to the south, attacks Israel and takes captives. This is the same region where Israel had been defeated years earlier.

f.g: A Canaanite city in the Negev; archaeologists have excavated a site of that name east of Beersheba.
Hebrew Negev — the dry southern region of Canaan.

chapters.n: Israel vows to the Lord: if He gives them victory, they will completely devote these cities to Him, keeping none of the spoil for themselves.

f.g: Hebrew ḥaram — to devote wholly to God, usually by destruction, so no one profits from the war.

chapters.n: The Lord answers, and Israel wins. The place is named Hormah, meaning “destruction.” Notice the contrast: where they once lost by going without God (14:45), now they win by relying on Him.
Because Edom refused passage, Israel must take a long, hot detour around its territory. The people grow deeply discouraged by the hard road.

f.w: the soul of the people was much discouraged
f.g: Literally “the soul of the people grew short” — they ran out of patience.

chapters.n: Again they complain against God and Moses, even calling the manna “light bread” — worthless food. They despise the very miracle that kept them alive.

f.g: Contemptible, worthless bread — their insulting name for manna.

chapters.n: The Lord sends venomous snakes; many people die. “Fiery” may describe the burning pain of their bite.

f.g: Hebrew seraphim — “burning ones,” likely named for the burning effect of their venom.

chapters.n: This time the people admit their sin and ask Moses to pray for them. Moses, once again, intercedes for those who criticized him.

f.g: A rare, honest confession from the wilderness generation.

chapters.n: God does not simply remove the snakes. Instead He tells Moses to make a bronze serpent on a pole: anyone bitten who looks at it will live. Healing comes through faith-filled looking.
Moses makes the bronze serpent, and whoever looks lives. Jesus taught that this pointed to Him lifted on the cross; the Book of Mormon adds that many refused to look because it seemed too simple.
Israel moves on and camps at Oboth. The trip toward Moab continues.
They next camp at Ije-abarim, east of Moab, toward the sunrise.

f.g: “Ruins of Abarim” — on the edge of Moab.

chapters.n: Next they camp in the valley of Zared, a stream marking Moab’s southern border.

f.g: Also spelled Zered — a valley running into the southern Dead Sea.

chapters.n: They camp beyond the Arnon River, the border between Moab and the Amorite kingdom to the north.

f.g: A deep river gorge flowing west into the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: The writer quotes a lost ancient book, “the book of the wars of the LORD,” probably a collection of victory songs. The Bible sometimes cites sources it did not preserve.

f.w: book of the wars of the LORD
f.g: A lost record; compare the book of Jasher in Joshua 10:13.

chapters.n: The quotation describes the streams flowing toward Ar, a town on Moab’s border.

f.g: A Moabite city or region, mentioned again in Deuteronomy 2:9.

chapters.n: At Beer (meaning “well”), God promises water without anyone needing to complain first — a happy change.
Israel sings a joyful song to the well. After so much murmuring about water, here is gratitude.

f.g: An ancient work song, perhaps sung while digging or drawing water.

chapters.n: The leaders dug the well with their staffs under Moses’ direction. Then the people traveled on to Mattanah, whose name means “gift.”

f.g: Probably Moses, or a leader with a ruler’s staff.

chapters.n: The journey continues through Nahaliel and Bamoth.

f.g: “High places” — perhaps the same as Bamoth-baal (22:41).

chapters.n: They reach the heights of Pisgah overlooking the wasteland. From a Pisgah peak Moses would later view the promised land before he died.

f.g: “Wasteland” or desert, perhaps the barren area northeast of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: Israel sends messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who ruled north of the Arnon.
The request is just like the one to Edom: let us pass on the main road, touching nothing.

f.g: The major trade route east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: Sihon refuses and attacks Israel at Jahaz.
Israel defeats Sihon and takes his land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers. They stop at Ammon’s border, which was strongly defended (and which God told them not to attack).

f.g: A river flowing west into the Jordan; Jacob wrestled there (Genesis 32:22).

chapters.n: Israel settles in the Amorite cities, including Heshbon, Sihon’s capital.

f.g: An important city east of the Jordan, near modern Hisban in Jordan.

chapters.n: Sihon had himself taken this land from an earlier king of Moab. So Israel did not take Moab’s land — they took land Sihon had already conquered.
Now the writer quotes a popular poem from the bards (“they that speak in proverbs”), likely an Amorite victory song once celebrating Sihon over Moab.
The poem pictures fire spreading from Heshbon, burning up Moab. Israel retells it with a twist: the conqueror has now been conquered.

f.g: Hilltop sites, often used for worship.

chapters.n: Moab is mourned as defeated, and their god Chemosh portrayed as powerless to save his people. The point: false gods cannot protect.

f.g: The national god of Moab (1 Kings 11:7).

chapters.n: The song ends describing ruin stretching from Heshbon to Dibon and Medeba — towns across the region.

f.g: A Moabite town where the famous Moabite Stone (Mesha inscription) was found.

chapters.n: Israel now lives in the former Amorite land.
Moses sends spies to Jaazer and takes its villages, driving out the Amorites.

f.g: A town north of Heshbon in good grazing land (Numbers 32:1).

chapters.n: Israel turns north toward Bashan, and Og, its king, marches out to fight them at Edrei.

f.g: A fertile high plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its cattle and oaks.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Moses not to fear Og: He has already given him into Israel’s hand. God’s word comes before the battle.
Israel defeats Og and possesses his land. These victories over Sihon and Og were remembered for generations as proof that God fights for His people.
Israel camps on the plains of Moab, just across the Jordan from Jericho. They will stay here through the end of Deuteronomy, at the very edge of the promised land.

f.g: The lowlands northeast of the Dead Sea, east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: Balak, king of Moab, has seen Israel crush the Amorites and grows alarmed.
Moab is terrified because Israel is so numerous — even though God had told Israel not to attack Moab.
Moab’s leaders tell the Midianite elders that Israel will devour everything like an ox grazing a field. Moab and Midian join forces against Israel.

f.g: A desert people descended from Abraham and Keturah; Moses’ father-in-law Jethro was a Midianite.

chapters.n: Balak sends for Balaam, a famous non-Israelite seer from Pethor near the Euphrates. An Aramaic inscription found at Deir Alla in Jordan mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor, showing his fame.

f.g: A town in northern Mesopotamia, near “the river” — the Euphrates.

chapters.n: Balak asks Balaam to curse Israel, believing Balaam’s words carry power. In the ancient world a curse was thought to be a real force — but this story shows only God decides who is blessed.

f.w: he whom thou blessest is blessed

chapters.n: The elders bring payment for his services. The money will become Balaam’s great temptation.

f.g: The fee paid to a seer for cursing or fortune-telling.

chapters.n: Balaam tells them to stay overnight while he seeks the Lord’s answer. Surprisingly, he uses Israel’s covenant name for God, “the LORD” (Jehovah).
God comes to Balaam with a question — not because He doesn’t know, but to make Balaam examine what he is doing.

f.w: What men are these with thee?

chapters.n: Balaam explains that Balak, king of Moab, sent the messengers.
He repeats Balak’s request to curse the people who came out of Egypt.
God’s answer is clear: do not go, and do not curse Israel, for they are blessed.
Balaam sends the messengers home, explaining that the Lord won’t let him go. Notice he doesn’t say the people are blessed — perhaps hoping for another chance.
The princes report back to Balak that Balaam refused.
Balak tries again with more and higher-ranking officials, raising the pressure.
The new envoys urge Balaam not to let anything stop him.
Balak offers great honor and a blank check — anything Balaam asks.

f.w: promote thee unto very great honour

chapters.n: Balaam’s reply sounds noble: even a palace full of silver and gold couldn’t make him go beyond God’s word. His words are right, but his heart seems tempted.

f.w: I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD

chapters.n: Yet he asks them to stay another night to see whether God will say “more.” He already had God’s answer; asking again shows he hoped it would change.
God permits Balaam to go, but only to speak what God gives him. Sometimes God allows what we keep pressing for, to teach us its consequences.
Balaam saddles his donkey and leaves with the princes of Moab.
God is angry because Balaam went with the wrong heart — eager for reward. The angel of the Lord blocks his path as an adversary.

f.g: Hebrew satan — “one who opposes”; here God’s own angel stands in opposition.

chapters.n: The donkey sees the angel with drawn sword and swerves into a field. Balaam, who claimed to be a seer, sees nothing and beats her.
The angel stands in a narrow path between vineyard walls.
The donkey presses against a wall, crushing Balaam’s foot, and he beats her again.
The angel moves to a spot so narrow there is no way around.
The donkey simply lies down. Furious, Balaam beats her with his staff. Each step the path gets narrower — like a conscience closing in.
Then the Lord opens the donkey’s mouth, and she asks why he has beaten her three times. Peter later wrote that the “dumb ass” rebuked the prophet’s madness.

f.w: the LORD opened the mouth of the ass

chapters.n: Balaam, without even being surprised, says he would kill her if he had a sword — not realizing an angel with a sword is standing right there.
The donkey reasons with him: has she ever acted like this before? Balaam admits she hasn’t. The animal shows more wisdom than her master.

f.w: was I ever wont to do so
f.g: wont = accustomed; “Have I ever done this before?”

chapters.n: The Lord opens Balaam’s eyes, and he sees the angel. He falls face down. True sight is a gift from God.
The angel says he came to oppose Balaam because his path was reckless — headed in the wrong direction morally.

f.g: Reckless, crooked, contrary to God’s will.

chapters.n: The donkey saved his life three times. Had she not turned aside, the angel would have killed Balaam and spared her.
Balaam admits his sin and offers to go home. His repentance seems sincere in the moment, though later events show his heart remained divided.
The angel tells him to go on — but to speak only what God gives. The rest of the story will prove that God’s word cannot be bought.
Balak eagerly meets Balaam at Moab’s border on the Arnon.
Balak complains that Balaam took too long. Doesn’t he know Balak can richly reward him?
Balaam warns that he can only speak what God puts in his mouth. He has no power of his own to curse.

f.w: the word that God putteth in my mouth

chapters.n: They travel together to Kirjath-huzoth, a town in Moab.

f.g: “City of streets”; its location is unknown.

chapters.n: Balak offers sacrifices of oxen and sheep, sharing the meat with Balaam and the princes — a ceremonial feast before the cursing.
Next morning Balak takes Balaam to the high places of Baal, where he can see the edge of Israel’s camp. Balak believes seeing the people will help the curse work.

f.g: Possibly a place name, Bamoth-baal — hilltop shrines to the Canaanite god Baal.

chapters.n: Balaam orders seven altars and seven bulls and rams. Seven, the number of completeness, was meant to make the ritual as powerful as possible.
Balak and Balaam offer a bull and a ram on each altar. They are trying to win God over with sacrifice — as if He could be bribed.
Balaam leaves Balak by the offerings and goes alone to a bare height, hoping the Lord will meet him there.

f.g: A hilltop; some translate “a barren height.”

chapters.n: God meets Balaam, who points to the seven altars he has prepared — as though reminding God of his offerings.
The Lord puts His own words in Balaam’s mouth and sends him back. The message will not be Balaam’s own.

f.w: put a word in Balaam's mouth

chapters.n: Balaam returns to find Balak and the Moabite princes waiting eagerly beside the sacrifice.
Balaam begins his first oracle in poetry. He recalls being summoned from Aram in the east to curse Jacob. “Jacob” and “Israel” are parallel names for the same people.

f.g: Here, a solemn poetic oracle or prophetic saying (Hebrew mashal).
Syria and northern Mesopotamia, northeast of Canaan.

chapters.n: The heart of the message: how can he curse those God has not cursed? No human word can override God’s blessing.

f.w: How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?

chapters.n: From the hilltop he sees Israel as a people set apart, not just one more nation. Israel’s distinctiveness came from its covenant with God.
Israel is as countless as dust, fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham. Balaam even wishes to die like these righteous people — a wish tragically unfulfilled (31:8).

f.w: Let me die the death of the righteous

chapters.n: Balak is shocked: he hired Balaam to curse, and instead got a full blessing.
Balaam answers that he must speak whatever the Lord gives him.
Balak tries a new location where Balaam will only see part of Israel — perhaps thinking a smaller view will weaken the blessing.
They go to the field of Zophim on Pisgah, and the seven-altar ritual is repeated.
Balaam again goes off to meet the Lord.
The Lord again puts a message in Balaam’s mouth.
Balak, waiting by his offering, asks what the Lord said. Even the Moabite king now uses the name of Israel’s God.
Balaam’s second oracle begins with a call for Balak to listen closely.
One of the great statements of God’s faithfulness: He is not like humans who lie or change their minds. What He promises, He does.

f.w: God is not a man, that he should lie

chapters.n: God has blessed, and Balaam cannot undo it.
God sees no iniquity in Israel — not because they were sinless, but because He chose to look on them as His covenant people. He is with them as their King.

f.g: The cheering of a people for their king — here, the Lord as Israel’s King.

chapters.n: God brought them from Egypt with the strength of a wild ox. “Unicorn” in the KJV is a mistranslation of a real animal, the wild ox.

f.g: Hebrew re’em — the wild ox (aurochs), a powerful horned animal, not a mythical creature.

chapters.n: No magic or omen works against Israel. People will say, “Look what God has done!” — the phrase later sent as the first telegraph message in 1844.

f.g: wrought = done, worked. Samuel Morse used these words in the first long-distance telegraph message.

chapters.n: Israel will rise like a lion that will not rest until victorious. The lion is an image later tied to Judah and to the Messiah.
Exasperated, Balak cries: then don’t curse them or bless them at all!
Balaam reminds him he had warned that he must speak whatever the Lord says.
Balak tries a third place, hoping God might allow a curse from there.
They go to the top of Peor, overlooking the wasteland — a name that will soon be linked with Israel’s sin (chapter 25).
Balaam again calls for seven altars, bulls, and rams.
Balak complies once more, offering a bull and ram on each altar. Three attempts, but God’s word will not change.
Balaam finally understands that the Lord wants to bless Israel. He stops seeking omens and simply looks toward Israel’s camp in the wilderness.

f.g: Omens or sorcery — the methods of pagan divination Balaam had used before.

chapters.n: He sees Israel camped by tribes in God’s appointed order, and the Spirit of God comes upon him. Even an imperfect man can be moved by God’s Spirit for His purposes.

f.w: the spirit of God came upon him

chapters.n: Balaam’s third oracle opens by describing himself as a man whose eyes have been opened — fitting, since the angel had to open his eyes on the road.

f.w: the man whose eyes are open

chapters.n: He has heard God’s words and seen a vision of the Almighty, falling down yet seeing clearly.

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai — an ancient name for God, as in El Shaddai (Genesis 17:1).
Not in the Hebrew; literally “falling down,” perhaps prostrate before God.

chapters.n: “How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob!” These words are still sung in Jewish synagogues as worship begins (the Ma Tovu).
Israel is pictured as lush gardens and trees beside water — a vision of a well-watered, flourishing people in a dry land, like Eden.

f.g: Aloe-wood trees, prized for their fragrance.

f.w: as gardens by the river's side

chapters.n: Overflowing water means abundance; Israel’s descendants will spread far. Israel’s king will be greater than Agag, a name used by Amalekite kings.

f.w: his seed shall be in many waters
f.g: His descendants will be many and well-provided — water symbolizing life and prosperity.

chapters.n: Repeating the second oracle’s image, Israel has the strength of a wild ox to overcome its enemies.

f.g: The wild ox, not a mythical creature.

chapters.n: Like a resting lion no one dares disturb, Israel is secure. Balaam ends with the promise God gave Abraham: those who bless Israel are blessed, and those who curse it are cursed — ironically, a warning to Balak himself.

f.w: Blessed is he that blesseth thee

chapters.n: Furious, Balak claps his hands in anger — he has paid for three curses and received three blessings.

f.g: A gesture of anger and scorn.

chapters.n: Balak orders Balaam home without reward, sarcastically blaming the Lord for keeping Balaam from honor.
Balaam reminds Balak of what he told the messengers from the start.
Even for a houseful of silver and gold, he could not do anything — good or bad — on his own; he must speak what the Lord says.

f.g: By my own choice or initiative.

chapters.n: Before leaving, Balaam offers one more prophecy, unasked: what Israel will do to Moab in the latter days.

f.g: Hebrew “the end of days” — the distant future.

chapters.n: His fourth oracle begins with the same solemn introduction.
He adds that he knew the knowledge of the Most High — a title for God as supreme over all.

f.g: Hebrew Elyon, a title for God (Genesis 14:18-20).

chapters.n: A famous messianic prophecy: a Star and a Sceptre (a king’s rod) will rise from Israel. It was first fulfilled in King David, who conquered Moab; Christians see its fullest meaning in Jesus Christ, the royal Son of David whose birth was announced by a star.

f.w: there shall come a Star out of Jacob

f.g: Possibly a name for a tribal group in Moab; some read it as “sons of tumult.”

chapters.n: Edom and Seir (its mountain country) will be conquered, while Israel triumphs. This came true under David.

f.g: The mountainous region of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: A ruler from Jacob will have dominion and destroy his enemies’ remnant.
Looking toward Amalek, Israel’s first attacker after the Exodus, Balaam foretells its eventual destruction.

f.w: Amalek was the first of the nations

chapters.n: He looks next at the Kenites, a people living in rocky strongholds. “Nest” (qen) is a wordplay on their name.

f.g: A clan related to Moses’ father-in-law (Judges 1:16).

chapters.n: Yet even the Kenites will be carried away when Assyria (Asshur) comes — a prophecy of the great empire that would one day dominate the region.

f.g: Assyria, the Mesopotamian empire that rose centuries later.

chapters.n: Balaam cries out: who can survive when God carries out these judgments?
Ships from Chittim (Cyprus, or more broadly the western sea peoples) will afflict Assyria and Eber, but they too will perish. Every empire rises and falls under God’s hand.

f.g: Kittim — originally Cyprus, later used for western sea powers such as Greece or Rome (Daniel 11:30).
Possibly peoples east of the Euphrates, or the Hebrews’ ancestral line (Genesis 10:21).

chapters.n: Balaam returns home and Balak goes his way. But the story isn’t over: Balaam’s advice will soon lead Israel into sin at Peor.
Where Balaam’s curses failed, temptation succeeded. Camped at Shittim, Israelite men begin sexual relationships with Moabite women — a betrayal of their covenant.

f.g: “Acacia trees” — Israel’s last camp east of the Jordan (Joshua 2:1).
Sexual immorality; it also led to spiritual unfaithfulness.

chapters.n: The women invite them to feasts for their gods, and the Israelites eat the sacrifices and bow to idols. Immorality opened the door to idolatry.
Israel “joined” itself to Baal of Peor, the local god — like being yoked to him. The Lord’s anger burns. Later scripture tells us this plan came from Balaam’s counsel.

f.g: The god Baal as worshiped at Mount Peor.

chapters.n: God orders the leaders responsible for this apostasy executed publicly. Leaders who led or allowed it were held accountable.

f.g: Probably the chiefs who took part in or allowed the idolatry.

chapters.n: Moses tells Israel’s judges to execute those under their authority who joined in Baal worship.
While people weep in repentance at the tabernacle, one Israelite brazenly brings a Midianite woman into the camp in full view of Moses and everyone — open defiance at the worst possible moment.

f.g: Midianite. Midian had joined Moab in plotting against Israel (22:4).

chapters.n: Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson and a young priest, rises from the crowd and takes a spear.
He follows the couple into the tent and kills them both, and the plague stops. It is a jarring scene; scripture presents it as zeal against open rebellion that threatened all Israel.

f.g: Possibly an inner chamber or a shrine-like tent.

chapters.n: Twenty-four thousand died in the plague. Paul, writing from memory or counting differently, mentions 23,000 in one day.
The Lord speaks to Moses about Phinehas.
Phinehas turned away God’s wrath because he shared God’s jealousy for His covenant. God’s “jealousy” is the protective love of a husband for a covenant bride.

f.g: In the Bible, God’s zeal to protect an exclusive covenant relationship (Exodus 20:5).

chapters.n: God gives Phinehas His “covenant of peace” — a promise of His favor and friendship.
Phinehas and his descendants receive a lasting priesthood. The high priests of later Israel, including Zadok, traced their line through him.

f.g: Here, removed the guilt that was bringing judgment on the people.

chapters.n: The man was Zimri, a leader of a chief family in the tribe of Simeon. His high rank made his act even more destructive.

f.g: Simeon’s tribe drops sharply in the next census (26:14), perhaps linked to this plague.

chapters.n: The woman was Cozbi, daughter of Zur, a Midianite chieftain. This was no chance encounter but involved Midian’s ruling families.
The Lord speaks again to Moses, now about the Midianites who planned Israel’s downfall.
God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies and strike them — the war is carried out in chapter 31.

f.g: vex = harass, treat as an enemy

chapters.n: The reason: Midian deliberately lured Israel into sin by trickery at Peor. Seduction, not swords, was their weapon — and it nearly worked where Balaam’s curses had failed.
After the plague at Peor, the Lord calls for a new census. The old generation has nearly passed, and a new Israel stands ready to enter the land. Eleazar now serves as high priest in Aaron’s place.
As in chapter 1, men twenty and older able to fight are counted by family. This count will be used for war and for dividing the land.
Moses and Eleazar give the order on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.
The census follows the Lord’s command, counting the descendants of those who came out of Egypt.
The list begins with Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, and his clans. Each clan takes its name from a son of Reuben.
Reuben’s other clans come from Hezron and Carmi.
Reuben totals 43,730 — down from 46,500 at Sinai.

f.w: forty and three thousand and seven hundred and thirty

chapters.n: A short family note introduces Eliab, son of Pallu.
Eliab’s sons include Dathan and Abiram, the Reubenites who joined Korah’s rebellion. The census pauses to remember them.
Their fate became a warning sign to Israel: the earth swallowed them, and fire consumed the 250.
A merciful detail: Korah’s sons did not die. Their descendants became temple singers, and eleven Psalms are titled “for the sons of Korah.”

f.w: the children of Korah died not

chapters.n: Simeon’s clans are listed by Simeon’s sons.
Two more Simeonite clans, from Zerah and Shaul.
Simeon counts just 22,200 — down from 59,300, the steepest drop of any tribe. Many think the Peor plague, led by a Simeonite prince, struck this tribe hardest.

f.w: twenty and two thousand and two hundred

chapters.n: Gad’s clans follow, beginning with Zephon, Haggi, and Shuni.
More Gadite clans from Ozni and Eri.
The clans of Arod and Areli complete Gad’s list.
Gad numbers 40,500, somewhat fewer than the 45,650 at Sinai.
Judah’s sons Er and Onan had died in Canaan long ago because of their wickedness, leaving no clans.
Judah’s clans come from Shelah, Pharez, and Zerah — the latter two born to Tamar.
Pharez’s sons Hezron and Hamul also form clans. From Hezron’s line would come King David — and Jesus Christ.
Judah is the largest tribe, 76,500 strong — up from 74,600. Judah’s leadership among the tribes is beginning to show.

f.w: threescore and sixteen thousand and five hundred

chapters.n: Issachar’s clans come from Tola and Pua.
Two more Issachar clans come from Jashub and Shimron, rounding out the tribe’s four families.
Issachar has grown to 64,300, from 54,400.

f.w: threescore and four thousand and three hundred

chapters.n: Zebulun’s three clans are listed, named for Sered, Elon, and Jahleel, Zebulun’s sons who went down to Egypt.
Zebulun numbers 60,500, a slight increase from 57,400.
Joseph’s descendants are counted as two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim, as Jacob had blessed them.
Manasseh’s line runs through Machir and his son Gilead, who gave his name to the region east of the Jordan where many of them settled.

f.g: Both a person and the hilly region east of the Jordan named for his clan.

chapters.n: Gilead’s sons form further clans, including Jeezer (Abiezer), Gideon’s ancestor.
Asriel and Shechem also head clans. A Manassite clan named Shechem shares its name with the famous city in Manasseh’s later territory.
Shemida and Hepher complete the list. Hepher’s line leads straight to Zelophehad and his daughters in the next verse.
A special note: Zelophehad had only daughters, named here. This sets up their brave request for an inheritance in the next chapter.
Manasseh numbers 52,700 — a large jump from 32,200.

f.w: fifty and two thousand and seven hundred

chapters.n: Ephraim’s clans are listed. Joshua belonged to this tribe.
Shuthelah’s son Eran forms another clan within Ephraim, showing how families branched over generations.
Ephraim counts 32,500, down from 40,500. Together, Joseph’s two tribes are the largest group.
Benjamin’s clans follow, from Bela, Ashbel, and Ahiram.
Two more Benjamite clans come from Shupham and Hupham. Spellings of these names vary slightly from list to list in the Bible.
Bela’s sons Ard and Naaman also head clans.
Benjamin has grown to 45,600, from 35,400.
Dan has just one clan listed, the Shuhamites — Dan had only one son recorded.
Though Dan had only one clan, it was large: 64,400 men — the second biggest tribe, up from 62,700.
Asher’s clans come from Jimna, Jesui, and Beriah.
Beriah’s sons Heber and Malchiel also head clans.
Asher’s daughter Sarah (Serah) is named — a rare mention of a woman in a census, suggesting she was well remembered.
Asher numbers 53,400, a solid gain from 41,500 at Sinai.
Naphtali’s clans are listed, beginning with Jahzeel and Guni, sons of Naphtali.
The remaining clans of Naphtali come from Jezer and Shillem, completing the twelve tribal lists.
Naphtali counts 45,400, fewer than the 53,400 counted forty years before.
The total is 601,730 — almost exactly the same as forty years earlier (603,550). God sustained the nation even as an entire generation passed away.

f.w: six hundred thousand and a thousand seven hundred and thirty

chapters.n: The Lord now explains how the census will be used.
The land will be divided according to the number of people in each tribe.
Larger tribes get more land, smaller tribes less — a fair distribution by need.
Yet the location of each tribe’s land will be decided by lot, leaving the choice in God’s hands.

f.g: Casting lots, a way of seeking God’s decision (Proverbs 16:33).

chapters.n: Size sets how much land; the lot sets where.
The Levites are counted separately by their three great clans: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Smaller Levite families are named, and the line of Kohath leads to Amram, father of Moses.
Amram’s wife Jochebed bore Aaron, Moses, and Miriam — the three great leaders of the Exodus.
Aaron’s four sons are listed. Only Eleazar and Ithamar carried on his priestly line.
Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire — another reminder of the cost of disregarding God’s ways.
Levite males from one month up numbered 23,000. They were counted apart because they received no tribal land.
This is the census taken by Moses and Eleazar on the plains of Moab.
Not one man from the first census remained — except as noted below. The generation that refused to enter had passed away.
God’s word came true: that generation died in the wilderness, except Caleb and Joshua, the two faithful spies. God’s promises — and warnings — are sure.

f.w: They shall surely die in the wilderness

chapters.n: Five sisters, the daughters of Zelophehad from the tribe of Manasseh, step forward. Their full family line is given to show their rightful place in Israel.
In a remarkable act of courage, these women stand before Moses, the high priest, the leaders, and the whole congregation at the tabernacle to make a request.

They explain that their father died in the wilderness for his own sins like the rest of his generation — but he was not a rebel with Korah, so his family should not lose its inheritance. He simply left no sons.

f.g: He died as part of the generation condemned in the wilderness, not for any special rebellion.

chapters.n: Why should their father’s name disappear just because he had no son? They ask for land among their father’s relatives so his family line continues.

f.g: A piece of land to own and pass on.

chapters.n: Moses doesn’t answer on his own; he takes their case to the Lord. Good leaders bring hard questions to God.
The Lord answers Moses about the sisters’ request — and His answer will change Israel’s law.
God says the daughters are right! They are to receive their father’s inheritance. God’s answer expands the law to protect women and families.
A new general law follows: when a man dies without sons, his inheritance goes to his daughters.
If he has no daughters, it goes to his brothers.
If no brothers, then to his father’s brothers (his uncles).
Otherwise, to his nearest relative. This becomes a permanent rule of justice in Israel, ensuring every family’s land stays within its clan.
The Lord tells Moses to climb Mount Abarim and view the land God has given Israel.

f.g: A mountain range east of the Dead Sea; Mount Nebo is one of its peaks (Deuteronomy 32:49).

chapters.n: After seeing it, Moses will die and be gathered to his people, as Aaron was. Latter-day Saint scripture adds that Moses was taken up rather than dying in the ordinary way.
The reason is repeated: at Meribah Moses failed to honor God as holy before the people.
Moses responds, not with a complaint about himself, but with concern for the people.
He asks the Lord, the Father of all spirits, to appoint a new leader over Israel.

f.w: God of the spirits of all flesh

chapters.n: Moses wants a leader who will go before the people in battle and daily life, so they won’t be like sheep without a shepherd. Jesus later used the same image of the crowds He loved.

f.w: as sheep which have no shepherd

f.g: Lead them in war and in daily affairs.

chapters.n: The Lord chooses Joshua, “a man in whom is the spirit,” and tells Moses to lay his hand on him — an ordinance of setting apart.
Joshua is to be presented before Eleazar and the whole congregation and given his charge publicly, so all know he is called.

f.g: A commission; instructions for his responsibilities.

chapters.n: Moses shares some of his authority with Joshua so that the people will follow him.
Joshua will seek God’s will through Eleazar, who uses the Urim to inquire of the Lord. Even the new leader must follow revelation.

f.g: A sacred instrument kept with the high priest’s breastplate for receiving revelation (Exodus 28:30).

chapters.n: Moses obeys, presenting Joshua before Eleazar and the congregation.
He lays his hands on Joshua and gives him his charge, as the Lord commanded. Leadership passes in an orderly way, by divine call and the laying on of hands.
With a new generation about to enter the land, the Lord gives a full calendar of public offerings (chapters 28–29).
God calls the offerings “my bread” — a way of describing the food of the altar. Israel must offer them faithfully at their proper times.

f.g: A figurative phrase; Israel knew God did not need food (Psalms 50:12-13).

chapters.n: Every day two flawless year-old lambs are offered as a “continual” burnt offering. Worship was to be steady and constant, not just occasional.
One lamb in the morning, one in the evening — bookending each day with devotion, like morning and evening prayers.
Each lamb is accompanied by a grain offering of fine flour mixed with high-quality oil.

f.g: A dry measure, roughly half a bushel to two-thirds of a bushel.
The finest olive oil, pressed by pounding rather than crushing.

chapters.n: This daily offering was first established at Mount Sinai.
A quarter-hin of strong drink is poured out for each lamb in the holy place.

f.g: A fermented drink; poured out, not drunk.

chapters.n: The evening lamb is offered just like the morning one, with the same grain and drink offerings.
On the Sabbath, the offering doubles: two extra lambs with their grain and drink offerings.
These Sabbath offerings are in addition to the daily ones — the holy day gets more, not less.
At each new moon (the start of each month), a large offering is made: two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs.

f.g: The new moon; Israel’s months followed the lunar cycle.

chapters.n: Each animal comes with its grain offering, scaled to size: three tenths for a bull, two for a ram.
One tenth for each lamb — the same proportions as in 15:4-9.
Wine offerings also scale by animal. This was the monthly offering throughout the year.
A goat is also offered as a sin offering each month, along with the daily offerings — a regular reminder that the people needed cleansing.
Passover comes on the fourteenth day of the first month, remembering the Exodus. It points to Christ, the Lamb of God.
The next day begins the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread.
The first day is a sacred assembly when no ordinary work is done.

f.g: A sacred gathering of the people for worship.

chapters.n: That day’s offering matches the new moon offering: two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs, all without blemish.
The grain offerings follow the usual pattern.
One tenth of flour for each of the seven lambs.
A goat for a sin offering makes atonement for the people.
All this is added to the regular morning offering.
The same offerings are repeated every day for the seven days of the feast.

f.g: Food — here the food of the altar offerings.

chapters.n: The seventh day is another sacred assembly with no ordinary work.

On the day of firstfruits — the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), seven weeks after Passover — Israel brings a new grain offering and holds a sacred assembly. The Holy Ghost was poured out on this feast day in Acts 2.

f.g: After counting seven weeks from Passover.

chapters.n: The burnt offering is two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs.
With grain offerings of three tenths per bull and two per ram.
Each of the seven lambs is matched with its own tenth of flour, just as at Passover.
A goat is offered to make atonement.
All these come on top of the daily offering, and all animals must be without blemish. Israel’s calendar was saturated with worship, each sacrifice pointing ahead to Christ’s perfect offering.
The seventh month (in early autumn) is Israel’s holiest month. It opens with a sacred assembly and the blowing of trumpets — a call to gather and prepare. Jews today celebrate this as Rosh Hashanah.
The burnt offering for the day: one bull, one ram, and seven flawless year-old lambs.
Their grain offerings follow the standard proportions.

f.g: Tenths of an ephah of flour.

chapters.n: One tenth of flour for each lamb.
A goat for a sin offering makes atonement — preparing hearts for the Day of Atonement ten days later.
All this comes in addition to the new-moon offerings and the daily offerings. On a holy day the sacrifices stack up, never replacing the regular ones.
The tenth day is the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur). The people “afflict their souls” — fast and humble themselves — and do no work at all.

f.w: tenth day of this seventh month

chapters.n: A burnt offering of one bull, one ram, and seven lambs is made.
Their grain offerings of flour and oil follow the same proportions as the first day of the month.
Each of the seven lambs again receives its tenth of flour.

A goat for a sin offering — in addition to the special atonement offerings of Leviticus 16, when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies. Hebrews sees in that day a type of Christ entering heaven for us.
On the fifteenth day begins the joyful seven-day Feast of Tabernacles (Booths), when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness and to thank God for the harvest.

f.w: keep a feast unto the LORD seven days

chapters.n: The first day has the largest offering of the whole year: thirteen bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs. The festival of joy is also the festival of abundance.

f.g: Over the seven days the bulls total 70; Jewish tradition linked that number to the seventy nations of the world (Genesis 10).

chapters.n: Each of the thirteen bulls and two rams has its grain offering.
And each of the fourteen lambs its tenth of flour.
A goat for a sin offering, besides the daily offering. Even in celebration, Israel remembered its need for atonement.
On day two, twelve bulls — one fewer — plus two rams and fourteen lambs. The bull count drops by one each day.
Their grain and drink offerings follow the established pattern for each animal.

f.g: According to the rule already given.

chapters.n: Again a goat for a sin offering, in addition to the daily offerings.
Day three: eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen lambs.
With their proper grain and drink offerings.
And a goat for a sin offering.
Day four: ten bulls, two rams, fourteen lambs.
The grain and drink offerings match their number.
A sin offering goat, along with the daily sacrifices.
Day five: nine bulls, two rams, fourteen lambs.
The grain and drink offerings again scale with the number of animals.
Another goat is offered for sin. Every single day of the feast included a reminder of the need for atonement.
Day six: eight bulls, two rams, fourteen lambs.
Their accompanying grain and drink offerings are prepared as before.
And the goat for a sin offering.
Day seven: seven bulls — the number of completeness, fittingly on the seventh day of the seventh month.
With grain and drink offerings in proportion.
A final goat for a sin offering of the seven-day feast.
An eighth day follows as a closing solemn assembly, a day of rest. On “the last day, that great day of the feast,” Jesus invited the thirsty to come unto Him.

f.g: A closing sacred gathering. In Latter-day Saint usage the phrase also names a special meeting to sustain Church leaders.

chapters.n: The eighth day’s offering returns to a modest one bull, one ram, and seven lambs.
The bull, ram, and lambs each come with their grain and drink offerings.
And a goat for a sin offering, besides the daily offering.
These are the required public offerings at the appointed feasts. Individuals could add their own vows, freewill gifts, and peace offerings — personal worship on top of community worship.

f.g: Voluntary gifts given from the heart.

chapters.n: Moses passes all these commandments on to Israel exactly as the Lord gave them.
Following the laws on freewill offerings and vows, Moses addresses the tribal leaders about how vows work.

f.g: Tribal leaders responsible for applying the law.

chapters.n: The basic rule: a man who makes a vow or oath to the Lord must keep his word completely. Promises made to God are sacred.

f.w: bind his soul with a bond
f.g: Make a solemn commitment that obligates him.

f.w: he shall not break his word

chapters.n: Special rules apply when a young unmarried woman living in her father’s home makes a vow.

f.g: While young and under her father’s household authority.

chapters.n: If her father hears the vow and says nothing, it stands. Silence means consent.

f.g: Remain silent, say nothing against it.

chapters.n: But if he objects on the day he hears it, her vow is cancelled, and the Lord releases her. In that household-based society, a father was responsible for his family’s commitments, especially ones affecting family property.
If a woman made a vow, even a rash one, before marriage and then marries, a related rule applies.
If her husband hears and says nothing that day, her vow stands.
If he objects that day, the vow is cancelled and the Lord forgives her. The rule protected a household from unexpected obligations while still taking vows seriously.
A widow or divorced woman has no husband or father over her vows, so she is fully bound by them herself — she is treated as independent and responsible.
If a married woman makes a vow while living in her husband’s house,
and her husband hears and doesn’t object, it stands.
If he cancels it on the day he hears, it does not stand, and the Lord forgives her.
A husband may confirm or cancel any vow or oath of self-denial (such as fasting) that his wife makes.
If he says nothing day after day, his silence confirms all her vows.
But if he cancels them later, after having let them stand, he bears the guilt for her broken vow. The responsibility shifts to him — a check against misuse of this authority.
These are the Lord’s rules about vows in families. Underneath them is one principle: words spoken to God matter, and families share responsibility for keeping them.
The Lord speaks to Moses about one last task before his death.
Israel is to take vengeance on the Midianites for luring them into sin at Peor (chapter 25). After this, Moses will die.

f.g: A gentle way of speaking of death and joining one’s ancestors.

chapters.n: Moses calls for soldiers to carry out “the LORD’s vengeance.” The war is presented as divine judgment, not personal revenge.

f.g: Carry out the Lord’s justice on Midian.

chapters.n: Each tribe sends a thousand men, so the whole nation shares the task.
Twelve thousand are chosen — a small army, showing the victory would depend on God rather than numbers.
Phinehas, the priest who had stopped the plague at Peor, goes with them, carrying sacred objects and trumpets to sound in battle.
Israel fights Midian and kills the men. Midian still appears later in Israel’s history (Judges 6), so this likely concerned the particular Midianite groups involved at Peor.

Five Midianite kings die, including Zur, father of Cozbi. Balaam is also killed — the prophet who blessed Israel with his mouth but plotted against them with his counsel. He did not die “the death of the righteous” he once wished for.

f.w: Balaam also the son of Beor

chapters.n: Women, children, livestock, and goods are taken as captives and spoil.
Their towns and encampments are burned so that Midian’s settlements in the area are removed.

f.g: Their fine encampments or fortified settlements.

chapters.n: All the captives and plunder, people and animals alike, are gathered to be brought back to camp.
Everything is brought to Moses, Eleazar, and the congregation at the camp on the plains of Moab.
Leaders go out to meet the army outside the camp, since soldiers who had touched the dead were unclean.
Moses is angry with the officers returning from battle.
He asks why they spared all the women.
These Midianite women, following Balaam’s advice, had deliberately seduced Israel into idolatry at Peor, causing the deadly plague. Revelation also remembers “the doctrine of Balaam.”

Moses orders the death of the boys and of women who had been sexually active. This is one of the hardest passages in scripture for modern readers. The text frames it as removing the source of the Peor apostasy; faithful readers have long wrestled with it honestly.

f.g: Had sexual relations with a man.

chapters.n: The young girls are spared and taken into Israelite households, likely as servants or eventual wives.
Soldiers and captives must stay outside the camp seven days and be purified on the third and seventh days, because they had touched the dead.
All clothing and items of leather, goat hair, and wood must also be purified.
Eleazar the priest explains the purification law to the soldiers.
Metal objects — gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, and lead — need special cleansing.

f.g: In the KJV, usually bronze (copper alloy).

chapters.n: Metals that can withstand fire pass through fire, then are sprinkled with the water of purification. Things that would burn are washed in water.
On the seventh day they wash their clothes, become clean, and may return to the camp.
The Lord gives instructions for dividing the spoil.
Moses, Eleazar, and the family heads are to count everything taken.
The spoil is split in half: half for the 12,000 soldiers and half for the rest of the community. Those who stayed home share in the victory — a principle David later followed.

f.w: divide the prey into two parts

chapters.n: From the soldiers’ half, one in every five hundred goes to the Lord as a tribute.
This share goes to Eleazar the priest as an offering to the Lord.
From the congregation’s half, one in fifty goes to the Levites who serve at the tabernacle. Those who did not fight give at a higher rate.
Moses and Eleazar do as the Lord commanded.
The livestock totals were enormous: 675,000 sheep...
…72,000 cattle. The size of the herds shows how wealthy these Midianite groups were.
…61,000 donkeys, the main pack animals of the desert peoples.
…and 32,000 young women and girls, who were taken into Israel’s households.
The soldiers’ half was 337,500 sheep. A small army received half, so each soldier’s share was large.
The Lord’s share of the sheep was 675 — exactly one in five hundred.
Of 36,000 cattle, 72 went to the Lord.
Of 30,500 donkeys, 61 went to the Lord.
Of 16,000 persons, 32 were given to the Lord’s service — likely to work at the sanctuary.
Moses gives the Lord’s portion to Eleazar, as commanded.

f.g: A portion set apart for the Lord.

chapters.n: Now the congregation’s half is described — an equal share for those who stayed in camp.
It also had 337,500 sheep, exactly matching the soldiers’ half.
…36,000 cattle, the same as the soldiers received.
…30,500 donkeys, again an exact half of the total.
…and 16,000 persons. The careful bookkeeping shows the spoil was divided fairly.
Moses gives one in fifty from the congregation’s half to the Levites.
The army officers come to Moses with a report.
Astonishingly, not a single Israelite soldier was lost. The officers see this as a miracle.

f.w: there lacketh not one man of us

chapters.n: In gratitude they bring a voluntary offering of gold jewelry to make atonement for themselves — perhaps recalling that a census required a ransom so no plague would come.

f.w: to make an atonement for our souls

chapters.n: Moses and Eleazar accept the gold, all crafted jewelry.
The officers’ gold weighs 16,750 shekels — around 400 pounds.

f.g: A shekel weighed about 11 grams (0.4 ounce).

chapters.n: A note explains that ordinary soldiers kept their own plunder.
The gold is placed in the tabernacle as a memorial before the Lord — a lasting thank-you for His protection.

f.g: A reminder kept before God and the people.

chapters.n: The tribes of Reuben and Gad own huge herds. Looking at the grasslands of Jazer and Gilead east of the Jordan, they see ideal ranch country.

f.g: The hilly, fertile region east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: They bring a request to Moses, Eleazar, and the tribal leaders.
They list the towns of the conquered Amorite land they want, including Heshbon, Dibon, and Nebo.

f.g: A town named for the nearby mountain (or the Babylonian god Nabu).

chapters.n: The Lord gave Israel this land in battle, they note, and it is perfect for cattle — and they have cattle.
Their request: give us this land, and don’t make us cross the Jordan. It sounds like they want to settle down while everyone else fights.

f.g: A polite way to ask for a favor.

chapters.n: Moses responds sharply: should your brothers go to war while you sit here?
Why discourage everyone else from entering the land God gave them? Moses fears a repeat of history.
This is exactly what their fathers did at Kadesh-barnea forty years ago.
The spies saw the valley of Eshcol and its giant grapes, yet spread fear that turned the people back.
The Lord was angry and swore an oath that day.
No adult who came out of Egypt would see the promised land, because they did not wholeheartedly follow Him.
Except Caleb and Joshua, who did follow the Lord fully. Caleb was a Kenizzite, from a family that joined Judah — another sign that faith, not birth, mattered most.

f.g: Kenizzite — a clan that became part of the tribe of Judah.

chapters.n: So Israel wandered forty years until that whole generation died.
Moses warns that the sons are rising up as a new “brood of sinners,” ready to provoke God’s anger again.
If they turn away, God might leave Israel in the wilderness again — and they would be to blame for destroying the nation. One group’s choice can affect everyone.
Reuben and Gad propose a compromise: they will build pens for their animals and towns for their families here first.
But the men will go armed in front of Israel until all the tribes have their land, leaving their families in fortified towns.
They promise not to return home until every tribe has received its inheritance.
They will claim no land west of the Jordan, since their share lies east.

f.g: The far side — west of the Jordan.

chapters.n: Moses agrees — on condition. If they go to war armed “before the LORD”…

f.g: In God’s presence and under His direction, as in a holy war.

chapters.n: …crossing the Jordan until the Lord drives out His enemies…
…then they may return guiltless, and the land will be theirs. Their promise must be kept to God and to Israel.
But if they fail, they sin against the Lord — and “be sure your sin will find you out.” Hidden failures eventually come to light.

f.w: be sure your sin will find you out

chapters.n: Build your towns and pens, says Moses, but do what you have promised.
The leaders of Gad and Reuben agree to do as Moses commands.
Their families and animals will stay in Gilead.
But every fighting man will cross over to battle.
Since Moses will not live to see it, he gives instructions to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders.
If Gad and Reuben fight alongside them until the land is conquered, they are to receive Gilead.
If not, they must take their land in Canaan with everyone else.
Gad and Reuben repeat their commitment publicly, promising to do just as the Lord has said.
They pledge again to cross armed into Canaan. They kept this promise, as Joshua later confirmed.
Moses gives the lands of Sihon and Og to Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh — who are mentioned here for the first time.
Gad rebuilds the towns of Dibon, Ataroth, and Aroer north of the Arnon River.

f.g: The Moabite Stone, found here, mentions the “men of Gad” living in Ataroth.

chapters.n: Gad also builds Atroth-shophan, Jaazer, and Jogbehah, spreading northward into Gilead.
Including fortified towns and sheep pens, just as they said.
Reuben rebuilds Heshbon, Sihon’s old capital, along with Elealeh and Kirjathaim.
Some towns bore names of pagan gods like Nebo and Baal, so the Israelites renamed them — rejecting idolatry even in place names.

f.g: Probably because names like Nebo and Baal-meon honored false gods.

chapters.n: Machir’s descendants, of Manasseh, conquer Gilead and drive out the Amorites.
Moses gives Gilead to the clan of Machir.
Jair captures villages and names them Havoth-jair, “the tent villages of Jair.”
Nobah captures Kenath and renames it after himself. These eastern tribes settle the land, though its separation by the Jordan would later bring challenges.

f.g: A Manassite leader; the town name Nobah later reappears in Judges 8:11.

chapters.n: Here begins a travel log of Israel’s journey from Egypt to the Jordan — about forty stops. It is a record of God’s faithful leading through every stage.
Moses wrote this list at the Lord’s command. Keeping records of how God has led us helps us remember His goodness.
Israel left Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after Passover, marching out boldly — “with a high hand” — as the Egyptians watched.
Meanwhile the Egyptians were burying their firstborn. The plagues were judgments against Egypt’s gods, showing them powerless before the Lord.

f.w: upon their gods also the LORD executed judgments

chapters.n: From Rameses they camped at Succoth, the first stop after leaving their homes in Egypt.
Next to Etham, at the edge of the desert.
Then they turned back toward Pi-hahiroth, near Baal-zephon and Migdol — boxing themselves in by the sea, just as God planned.
They passed through the middle of the sea on dry ground, then traveled three days to Marah, where bitter water was made sweet.

f.w: passed through the midst of the sea

chapters.n: At Elim they found twelve springs and seventy palm trees — a welcome oasis.
They camped by the Red Sea — likely the Gulf of Suez.
Next the wilderness of Sin, where manna first fell.
On to Dophkah, a stop not mentioned in Exodus.
Then Alush, another stop known only from this list.
At Rephidim there was no water; God gave water from the rock, and Israel fought Amalek.
They reached the wilderness of Sinai, where they received the law and built the tabernacle — nearly a year’s stay.
From Sinai to Kibroth-hattaavah, “graves of craving,” where those who lusted for meat died.
Then Hazeroth, where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses.
Next Rithmah. Verses 18–36 list stops during the long wandering years, most of them otherwise unknown. The name may mean “broom bush,” a desert shrub.
Then Rimmon-parez. Rimmon means “pomegranate,” perhaps describing what grew there.
On to Libnah, a name meaning “white.”
Then Rissah. These obscure names are a reminder that God was with Israel even in the long, uneventful years.
Next Kehelathah, a name possibly meaning “assembly.”
Then Mount Shapher, a peak whose name may mean “beauty” or “pleasantness.”
On to Haradah, a name possibly related to “trembling.”
Then Makheloth, possibly “assemblies” — perhaps a usual gathering place for desert travelers.
Next Tahath. Its location, like most stops in this section, is now unknown.
Then Tarah, another wilderness campsite remembered only here.
On to Mithcah, perhaps meaning “sweetness” — maybe a place of good water.
Then Hashmonah, an unidentified stop in the desert south of Canaan.
Next Moseroth. Deuteronomy links nearby Mosera with Aaron’s death, likely referring to the general area of Mount Hor.
Then Bene-jaakan, “the sons of Jaakan,” possibly named for a clan with wells there.
Then Hor-hagidgad, probably the Gudgodah mentioned in Deuteronomy 10:7.
On to Jotbathah, described in Deuteronomy as a land of flowing streams.
Next Ebronah, on the way south toward the Gulf of Aqaba.
Then Ezion-gaber, at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba — later King Solomon’s seaport.
Back to the wilderness of Zin at Kadesh, where Miriam died and Moses struck the rock.
From Kadesh to Mount Hor on Edom’s border.
Aaron died on Mount Hor at the Lord’s command, on the first day of the fifth month of the fortieth year after the Exodus. This list gives the exact date.
Aaron was 123 years old — three years older than Moses, who died at 120.

f.w: an hundred and twenty and three years old

chapters.n: A reminder of the Canaanite king of Arad, who heard Israel was coming and attacked.
From Mount Hor they traveled to Zalmonah, beginning the long detour around Edom.
Then Punon, a copper-mining area — perhaps where the bronze serpent was made.

f.g: Likely Feinan in Jordan, a major ancient copper-mining site.

chapters.n: On to Oboth, already mentioned in the account of the march toward Moab.
Then Ije-abarim on Moab’s southern border — Israel has nearly reached the plains of Moab.
From Iim (short for Ije-abarim) to Dibon-gad, the town Gad later rebuilt.
Next Almon-diblathaim, a town in Moab mentioned centuries later by Jeremiah as Beth-diblathaim.
Then the mountains of Abarim near Nebo — where Moses would view the promised land.
Finally, the plains of Moab by the Jordan, opposite Jericho. The long journey is nearly over.
The camp stretched along the Jordan from Beth-jesimoth to Abel-shittim, a sprawling settlement.
On the plains of Moab, the Lord gives Moses instructions for entering Canaan.
When Israel crosses the Jordan into Canaan, a new set of responsibilities will begin.
...they must drive out the inhabitants and destroy their carved stones, metal idols, and hilltop shrines. Idolatry had to be removed completely.

f.g: Carved stone images or figured stones used in worship.
Idols made from melted, cast metal.

chapters.n: They are to take the land and live there, for God has given it to them.
The land is to be divided by lot and by tribe size, as in 26:52-56.
A warning: any inhabitants they allow to stay will become like thorns in their eyes and sides — constant trouble. The book of Judges shows this coming true.

f.w: pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides

chapters.n: Most sobering of all: if Israel adopts the Canaanites’ ways, God will treat Israel the way He planned to treat them. Israel’s later exile fulfilled this warning.

f.w: I shall do unto you, as I thought to do unto them

chapters.n: The Lord now describes the borders of the land Israel is about to inherit.
This is Canaan, the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and now about to “fall” to Israel by lot as their inheritance.

f.g: In KJV English, borders or territory.

chapters.n: The southern border begins in the wilderness of Zin, along Edom, starting from the southern end of the Dead Sea.

f.g: The Dead Sea, so salty that almost nothing lives in it.

chapters.n: It runs southwest past the Scorpion Pass, through Zin and south of Kadesh-barnea, to Hazar-addar and Azmon.

f.g: “Scorpions” — a steep pass southwest of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: From Azmon it bends to the Brook of Egypt and ends at the Mediterranean.

f.g: Not the Nile but a seasonal stream, usually identified with Wadi el-Arish in the northern Sinai.

chapters.n: The western border is the Mediterranean Sea.
The northern border starts at the Mediterranean and runs to Mount Hor — a different, northern mountain from the one where Aaron died, probably in the Lebanon range.

f.g: A northern peak, not the Mount Hor near Edom (20:22).

chapters.n: From there it extends to Lebo-hamath, the pass into Syria, and on to Zedad.

f.g: Possibly a place called Lebo-hamath, on the route toward the Syrian city of Hamath.

chapters.n: It continues to Ziphron and ends at Hazar-enan.
The eastern border runs from Hazar-enan to Shepham.
It goes down to Riblah and along the eastern shore of the Sea of Chinnereth — the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: The Sea of Galilee; the name may come from the Hebrew for “harp,” after its shape.

chapters.n: Then down the Jordan to the Dead Sea. These are the ideal borders; Israel only fully controlled this area under David and Solomon.
Moses tells Israel this western land will be divided by lot among the nine and a half tribes.
Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh have already received their land.
Their inheritance lies east of the Jordan, across from Jericho.
The Lord names the men who will divide the land.
Eleazar the priest and Joshua will lead — religious and civil leadership working together.
A leader from each tribe will help, so every tribe has a voice.
For Judah, Caleb — one of the two faithful spies, now about 85 years old. God kept His promise that he would enter the land.
For Simeon, Shemuel son of Ammihud. All these leaders except Caleb are new names — a new generation is taking charge.
For Benjamin, Elidad son of Chislon. Benjamin’s land would later include Jerusalem’s border region.
For Dan, Bukki son of Jogli. Dan’s first land assignment lay west of Benjamin toward the coast.
For Manasseh (one of Joseph’s two tribes), Hanniel son of Ephod.
For Ephraim, Joseph’s other tribe, Kemuel son of Shiphtan.
For Zebulun, Elizaphan son of Parnach. The list now moves to the northern tribes.
For Issachar, Paltiel son of Azzan, representing the tribe that would settle the fertile Jezreel valley.
For Asher, Ahihud son of Shelomi, whose tribe would settle along the northern coast.
For Naphtali, Pedahel son of Ammihud. The tribes are listed roughly south to north, the order in which their lands would lie.
These are the men the Lord appointed to divide the inheritance in Canaan. God’s promise is about to be fulfilled in practical, organized detail.
On the plains of Moab, the Lord speaks to Moses about the Levites’ homes and about justice for those who kill.
The Levites received no tribal land, so the other tribes must give them towns to live in, along with surrounding pasture.

f.g: Open pastureland around a town, not suburbs in the modern sense.

chapters.n: The Levites live in the towns, and the pastureland is for their cattle and other animals.
The pastureland extends about 1,000 cubits (roughly 1,500 feet) out from the town wall.

f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), the length from elbow to fingertip.

chapters.n: The total area is measured as 2,000 cubits on each side, with the town in the center. Scholars explain the two numbers in different ways, but the point is clear: a generous, defined area.
Six of these towns will be cities of refuge, where someone who accidentally kills another can flee. Forty-two more towns are added.

f.g: Someone who has killed a person.

chapters.n: Forty-eight Levite towns in all. Spreading the Levites through the land meant that teachers of God’s law lived among every tribe.
Larger tribes give more towns, smaller tribes fewer — everyone contributes fairly.
The Lord now explains the cities of refuge.
These laws apply once Israel crosses into Canaan.
Cities of refuge protect someone who kills a person accidentally.
The slayer is safe from the “avenger” — a relative of the dead person — until a fair trial is held. The law kept grief from turning into blind revenge.

f.g: Hebrew go’el — the next-of-kin responsible for family justice; the same word is also used for a “redeemer.”

chapters.n: There are to be six cities of refuge.
Three east of the Jordan and three in Canaan, so one is always within reach.

f.w: three cities on this side Jordan

chapters.n: The refuge is open to Israelites and foreigners alike — justice and mercy for everyone.
But refuge does not protect a murderer. Striking someone with an iron object that causes death counts as murder.
So does throwing a stone big enough to kill.
Or striking with a wooden weapon that can kill. The type of weapon helped show intent.
In a case of murder, the avenger of blood may put the killer to death.

f.g: The family member charged with seeking justice for the victim.

chapters.n: Pushing someone out of hatred, or ambushing and throwing something at them, is murder.
So is striking someone in hostility with one’s bare hand, causing death. Intent and hatred make the difference.
But if someone pushes another suddenly without hostility, or throws something without planning…
…or drops a stone without seeing the person and without any ill will — that is accidental killing.
The congregation acts as judge between the slayer and the avenger. A fair hearing comes before any penalty.

If the killing was accidental, the slayer is protected and must live in the city of refuge until the high priest dies. Many Christians see a picture of Christ here: the death of the High Priest sets the refugee free.

f.w: unto the death of the high priest

chapters.n: But if the slayer leaves the boundary of the refuge city…
…and the avenger finds and kills him outside it, the avenger is not guilty. Safety lay only inside the refuge.
The slayer must stay until the high priest dies; then he may go home to his own land.
These laws are permanent for every generation and place.
A murderer may be executed only on the testimony of witnesses — never on just one person’s word. This protected the innocent from false accusation.
No payment can buy off the penalty for murder. Human life is too precious to be priced in money.
Nor can a payment let an accidental slayer leave refuge early.
Bloodshed pollutes the land, and only justice upon the murderer can cleanse it. God takes the taking of life with utmost seriousness.
Do not defile the land, the Lord says, for I dwell among you. Israel’s laws of justice flowed from the fact that God lived in their midst.

f.w: I the LORD dwell among the children of Israel

chapters.n: The book closes by returning to Zelophehad’s daughters. Leaders from their clan in Manasseh come to Moses with a follow-up concern.
They recall that the Lord commanded the land be given by lot, and that Zelophehad’s inheritance go to his daughters.
If the daughters marry men of other tribes, their land would pass to those tribes, shrinking Manasseh’s share.

f.w: the tribe whereunto they are received
f.g: The tribe of the husbands they marry.

chapters.n: Even the Jubilee, which returned land to original families every fifty years, would not fix it — the land would be locked into the new tribe permanently.
Moses, speaking for the Lord, agrees: the leaders of Joseph’s tribe have raised a fair point.
The daughters may marry whomever they choose — but within their father’s tribe. Both their freedom and the tribe’s inheritance are respected.
This keeps each tribe’s land intact, honoring the original divisions God established.
The rule applies to every daughter who inherits land: she marries within her father’s tribe.
So land does not move from tribe to tribe, and each tribe keeps its own inheritance.
Zelophehad’s daughters obey the Lord’s command — faithful from first to last.
Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah marry their cousins.

f.g: Their cousins on their father’s side.

chapters.n: Their land stays within Manasseh. Joshua later records their receiving it, the promise fulfilled.
Numbers ends here: these are the laws the Lord gave through Moses on the plains of Moab, facing Jericho. Israel stands at the edge of the promise, ready for Moses’ final words in Deuteronomy.
